News.title: Britain defends seizing Putin’s shadow fleet tankers fuelling Ukraine war after tyrant threatened to ‘respond in kind’
News.content:
BRITAIN has defended its seizure of a Russian shadow fleet tanker after Vladimir Putin ominously threatened to “respond in kind”.

The beleaguered tyrant lashed out after one of his shadowy network of sanctioned vessels was captured in the English Channel.



Russia has been operating a shadow fleet of oil tankers to evade international sanctions, fuel its war-ravaged economy and fund its illegal war in Ukraine.

Elite Royal Marines Commandos boarded one such ship – The Smyrtos – and captured its 25 crew in a first-of- its-kind operation in June.



Dramatic footage of its seizure released by the MoD showed how marines fast-roped from helicopters during the six-hour operation.

The Smyrtos has since been anchored off Weymouth and its captain, Ajay Pant, has been charged with breaching Russian sanctions.

He has also been accused of directly or indirectly supplying or delivering prohibited Russian oil.

Putin blasted the seizure while overseeing Russian navy drills in the Pacific, branding the operation as “nothing other than piracy and banditry”.

The dictator menacingly warned that if Western countries seize more tankers, then Russian “will have to respond in kind”.

He added: “And not necessarily in the waters where raids on our ships and vessels are planned, but wherever we deem it necessary and appropriate, anywhere.”



His fleet commander Admiral Viktor Liina said he had identified 26 British commercial vessels since April in Russia’s exclusive economic zone.

Liina declared: “We have the capabilities to inspect and detain vessels from unfriendly states and their shadow fleet.

“We are ready to begin tackling these tasks.”



In response to Putin’s comments, the UK defended its seizure of the Smyrtos as being “in full accordance with international law“.

A government spokesperson said: “The UK is disrupting and deterring shadow fleet vessels and their harmful maritime activity which is fuelling Russia’s war with Ukraine.”

They added that, unlike Russia’s shadow fleet, Britain’s “armed forces and commercial vessels operate firmly in line with international maritime law”.

The UK’s Ministry of Defence has said that Russia operates more than 700 shadow tankers smuggling 75 per cent of its sanctioned oil.

To evade detection, they turn off tracking systems, falsify location data, and conduct ship-to-ship transfers at sea to disguise the oil’s origin.



These vessels – often older and poorly maintained – are accused of using complex ownership structures and flying under other nations’ flags to avoid detection.

The oil ferried is a “critical lifeline for the Kremlin” in “sustaining Russia’s illegal war” in Ukraine, the MoD said.

The Smyrtos continues to be detained and monitored by British authorities in Weymouth, while 22 of its 25 crew have been repatriated.



A Sun investigation revealed at least 28 ‘banned’ boats have been caught on radar transiting the channel since June 19.

It has sparked calls for more action from new PM Andy Burnham in the Channel to hit Russia‘s global oil trade empire where it hurts.

But Putin said he would be “forced to respond in kind,” if Russian ships continued to be targeted.

Retaliation would occur wherever the dictator “considers necessary and appropriate”, including “within the Pacific Fleet’s area of responsibility”.

Putin warned: “I would ask you to pay attention to this.



“The Defence Ministry has been given such an instruction, and I know that it has also been passed on to the Pacific Fleet command.”

Putin’s security council number two Dmitry Medvedev rammed home the Russian threat.

“The overwhelming majority of Western European vessels also sail under flags of convenience,” he said.

“And what does that mean?

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It means that, following a symmetrical approach, which is only fair, Russia has the right to attack any merchant vessel belonging to hostile countries, whether in our waters or in neutral waters, if there are sufficient grounds to suspect that it is carrying cargo in the interests of the enemy.



“In other words, any cargo at all.”

News.title: Karoline Leavitt’s best bits as WH press sec – from sparring with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, ‘your mom’ joke & ‘stupid’ jibe
News.content:
KAROLINE Leavitt has delivered plenty of fiery one-liners from the White House podium – and she is leaving the job on a high.

The 28-year-old press secretary is stepping down at the end of the month after 18 months as one of President Donald Trump’s most recognizable and trusted aides.



Trump announced her departure Wednesday, saying Leavitt wanted to spend more time with her family.

The president said it was “a decision I totally understand and respect!” and revealed she will remain in his orbit as “one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party.”



Leavitt, the youngest White House press secretary in history, described the job as “the honor and adventure of a lifetime.”

She added: “Most of all, I am thankful to the President for entrusting me with the distinct privilege of speaking on his behalf at the White House podium.



“I have relished holding the liberal media accountable and ensuring the American people hear the truth about President Trump’s successes.”

Her departure brings the curtain down on a lively stint behind the famous lectern that saw Leavitt repeatedly go viral for her clashes with the press.

From a two-word “your mom” comeback to fiery exchanges with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, here are some of her most memorable moments.

‘Your mom’

One of Leavitt’s cheekiest responses did not even come from the White House briefing room.



She went viral in October after sharing a text exchange with HuffPost White House correspondent S.V. Dáte as Trump prepared for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Hungary.

Dáte questioned the choice of Budapest as the proposed meeting place, pointing to its significance in relations between Russia and Ukraine.

“Does he not see why Ukraine might object to that site? Who suggested Budapest?” he asked.

Leavitt’s answer was short and sweet: “Your mom did.”



When Dáte questioned whether she thought the response was funny, Leavitt doubled down and branded him a “far-left hack who nobody takes seriously.

She added: “Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bulls*** questions.”

Kaitlan clash

CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins also found herself on the receiving end of a Leavitt broadside during one heated White House exchange.

Collins challenged the press secretary in March over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s criticism of media coverage of the deaths of American service members.



She claimed Hegseth was “complaining that it was front page news about these six service members who were killed.”

Leavitt immediately pushed back.

“That’s not what the secretary said, Kaitlan, and that’s not what the secretary meant,” she fired back.

“And you know it. You know you’re being disingenuous.”

Collins then read Hegseth’s full remarks and pointed out that news organizations report on US military deaths regardless of who occupies the White House.



But Leavitt wasn’t backing down.

“The press does only want to make the president look bad,” she said.

“That’s it. That’s a fact.”



‘Stupid question’

Another viral moment came during a June 2025 briefing when Leavitt was quizzed about Trump’s stance on demonstrations.

NOTUS reporter Jasmine Wright asked her to “clarify what kind of protest President Trump does support or find acceptable” after Trump issued a warning ahead of a military parade in Washington.

Leavitt replied that Trump “absolutely supports peaceful protests. He supports the First Amendment,” while stressing that “he does not support violence of any kind.”

Wright followed up by asking whether peaceful protests would be allowed on the day of the parade.

Leavitt appeared baffled that there was any doubt.



“Of course the President supports peaceful protests. What a stupid question,” she shot back.

Gulf row

Leavitt also went toe-to-toe with The Associated Press during a row that erupted over the newly renamed Gulf of America.

The Trump administration restricted the news agency’s access to some press events in early 2025 after the AP continued using Gulf of Mexico following Trump’s move to rename the body of water.

Leavitt defended the White House’s position as part of its push to hold news organizations accountable.

“It is a fact that the body of water off the coast of Louisiana is called the Gulf of America,” she declared.



The restrictions were later lifted.

But the AP found itself in Leavitt’s firing line again when reporter Josh Boak challenged Trump’s tariffs.

Boak asked why the president was “prioritizing tax hikes in the form of tariffs.”

Leavitt described them as a “tax hike on foreign countries,” prompting Boak to point out that tariffs are charged to importers.

That did not go down well.



“I think it’s insulting that you’re trying to test my knowledge of economics, and the decision that this President has made,” Leavitt responded.

Then came one final jab: “I now regret giving a question to The Associated Press.”

Leavitt will now swap the daily White House press battles for more time with her family, but she won’t be fully gone from Trump’s orbit.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The president has made clear he wants his outgoing press secretary close by as an outside adviser, meaning her headline-grabbing comebacks may not be over just yet.

News.title: Tricky A-level Maths question is dividing adults – but can YOU answer it?
News.content:
THOUSANDS of students have picked up their A-Level results today, but for many adults, it’s been decades since they last took a test.

As pupils open the results that may dictate the rest of their lives, do you have what it takes to succeed?



As A-Level results are released today (August 13), one TikTok user, @freemathstutor_uk, shared a seven-mark sum typically found towards the beginning of an A-Level maths paper.

Across major exam boards like Pearson, Edexcel and OCR, pupils will have to take three written maths exams, typically taking around two hours.



Each paper is worth 100 marks and features anywhere between 13 and 16 questions divided into multi-part sub-questions.

So, are you able to find the solution?

Question

A team game involves solving puzzles to escape from a room. Using data from the past, the mean time to solve the puzzles and escape from one of these rooms is 65 minutes with a standard deviation of 11.3 minutes.

After recent changes to the puzzles in the room, it’s claimed that the mean time to solve the puzzles and escape has changed. To test this claim, a random sample of 100 teams is selected.

The total time to solve the puzzles and escape for the 100 teams is 6,780 minutes. Assuming the times are normally distributed, test at the 2% level the claim that the mean time has changed.

The solution

According to past exam solutions, you’ll first need to define what a mean is.



This is the total of numbers divided by how many numbers there are, typically used as the best measure of an average.

Next, you should answer how the data is originally distributed, which should be able to set you up to calculate the rest of the question.

And if you said there was evidence to show the mean time is different, you would be correct.

The user, @freemathstutor_uk, told viewers: “We reject the H0 (null hypothesis) and there is sufficient evidence to show the mean time has changed.”

But remember, these papers typically go by the rule of a mark per minute, so for this 7-mark question, you should have only spent roughly 7 minutes on it in total.



In the comments, the video received mixed opinions. One user said: “I’m so cooked,” while another wrote: “So easy.”

So, were you able to solve it, or have you left your problem- solving days strictly in the past?

News.title: My daughter, 26, was absolutely happy before taking her own life day after vexatious complaint sparked by office gossip
News.content:
MUM'S TRAUMA My daughter, 26, was absolutely happy before taking her own life day after vexatious complaint sparked by office gossip

THE mum of a Treasury employee who took her own life has said her daughter was “absolutely happy” at work until office gossip sparked a “vexatious” complaint.

Chloe Moffat, 26, died on May 20 last year, a day after she was told by managers she had allegedly shared confidential information, an inquest heard on Monday.



The Treasury was found to have “materially contributed” to Chloe’s death by not informing her that the likely outcome if the allegations were true were a written warning – not a dismissal.

Mum Anne Moffat said Chloe had been “happy as Larry” in her role and not had any issues with her mental health prior to her death.



“She was so happy working there, absolutely happy. She was ready for a promotion and then there were some allegations made and Chloe denied them,” she told The Times.

She added that the complaints had been made by anonymous witnesses, who could “never have given a statement”.



“We know what the allegations were about — it was no more than office gossip, I’m sure it was all vexatious, sadly,” she said.

Assistant coroner Anna Crawford said at the Surrey Coroner’s Court that it was the general consensus that Chloe “enjoyed her job” and had an exemplary record.



Chloe had thought she was attending a routine check-in with her line manager on May 19, only to find a senior manager also present.

She was informed of allegations that she had shared highly sensitive information about colleagues, obtained as part of her job role – claims which she denied.

The managers told her no final decision had been made but that a formal investigation or disciplinary meeting might be needed.

When Chloe asked whether she’d lose her job, the senior manager said she “could not predict the outcome at this stage”.

She was temporarily removed from the director’s email inbox.



Chloe was reportedly shocked and upset during the meeting and texted a friend shortly afterwards, saying she thought she would be fired.

She also spoke with her mum, who tried to reassure her.

The following day, she took her own life.

The coroner said she would be sending a prevention of future deaths report to HM Treasury, the head of the civil service and to Acas.

A Treasury spokesperson said earlier this week: “We take the coroner’s concerns extremely seriously and recognise it is important to act quickly. We are now considering the findings carefully.

“We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again.”

News.title: US wife of Afghan migrant ‘suitcase killer’ is ‘completely convinced’ he killed Brit – as cops sit on bombshell CCTV
News.content:
THE distraught wife of the Afghan migrant accused of killing a Brit in Athens is “completely convinced” her partner is behind the aid worker’s death.

Alaina Hall, who shares a 16-month-old baby with murder suspect Sharif Ahmadzai, helped Greek cops arrest her husband after her brave testimony revealed crucial new details.



Alaina first met Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, in February 2026 after a volunteering mission for a refugee charity in Athens alongside Ahmadzai.

In her testimony Alaina described Elisabeth as “a very pleasant and sweet person, kind-hearted, with a good soul”.



The American also told cops she was “revolted” by her “very stubborn” husband and firmly believes he is Elisabeth’s killer, police sources told The Sun.

George Kalliakmanis, honorary head of the union of police officers in Greece, said Alaina has decided to stay in Athens with her baby but will have “nothing to do with” Ahmadzai ahead of his murder trial.



Kalliakmanis told The Sun: “She is completely convinced he did it. She has no desire to be mixed up with him.

“She wants nothing to do with him. She is appalled.”



A fellow volunteer added that the American was “never going to give Sharif the time of day again. Her thoughts, now, are with her [Elisabeth].”

During two rounds of questioning by Greek police, Alaina reportedly said: “Sharif is very persistent, very stubborn.

“Even if you put all the evidence, all the hard facts, right in front of him, he never admits anything.”

Police have footage allegedly showing the Afghan boxer transporting the Brit’s body in a suitcase via a cart-trolley, Kalliakmanis said.

He claims the video is unlikely to be released publicly, before adding: “It all boils down to one thing: motive. Why did he murder her, because that is what all the evidence points to.”



The married couple founded the NGO Love Every Nation a few years back but due to the chilling allegations, friends in the volunteer movement believe Alania is considering shutting it down.

Ahmadzai remains holed up in a hellish Greek jail – the notorious Korydallos prison – which is packed to the rafters with terrorists, rapists and murderers.

He is due to stay locked up until his trial which could still take months to begin as investigations continue.



Ahmadzai denies killing Elisabeth, but has confessed to stuffing her body in a suitcase and dumping it in a derelict building five minutes away from the flat where she was staying.

He has insisted he found the Scottish woman dead inside the apartment’s bathroom.

The Christian convert had keys to the flat because it was used as a regular meeting spot for the NGO with his wife.

The Afghan also confessed to withdrawing more than 10,000 euros with her credit cards.

Ahmadzai converted to Christianity within a year of arriving in Greece, but Alaina reportedly started questioning whether it was genuine or whether he had been trying to strengthen his refugee case.



Alaina’s friends believe that Lisa, who was a devout Christian herself, got caught up in the middle of the couple’s difficulties.

One theory is that Alaina may have confided in Lisa about her doubts, before the Brit confronted Ahmadzai and came under attack.

Authorities are still waiting for final toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissue that will determine Elisabeth’s exact cause of death.



Alaina reportedly told cops about her husband after she became suspicious he was involved in Elisabeth’s death.

Shortly after news broke that a woman’s body had been discovered inside a suitcase close to the couple’s home, Alaina recalled waking up with a “terrible” feeling.

In the morning she then texted Elisabeth and got two replies which made her suspicious.

Alaina said: “These messages were not in Lisa’s style, both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used.”

When she tried calling Elisabeth she didn’t get a reply.



Alaina also told police she had grown suspicious of her husband after she woke to find him missing on the evening of July 15.

When she checked his shared location, she saw he was in Elisabeth’s flat.

Having later confronted him, he told her he had been watching a football match but had gone to Elisabeth’s apartment to use the toilet.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She told police: “I don’t know what to tell you, but all of the above made me feel strange.

“Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband’s behaviour, I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable.”

News.title: Luxury £6.8million superyacht SINKS in the Med – just four days after being delivered to new owner
News.content:
A LUXURY £6.8million superyacht has sunk in the Mediterranean just four days after being delivered to its new owner.

Dramatic footage shows the lavish 98ft vessel slowly disappearing beneath the surface before rolling onto its side, leaving just a sliver of the yacht poking above the water.



The 30m Angiola II remained lying on the seabed, around 23ft below the surface, after a tense rescue operation lasting nearly three hours.

Sinking off Porto Cervo, Sardinia, the multi-million-pound vessel plunged beneath the surface between Cappuccini Island and Capo Ferro.



It had reportedly been handed to its Italian owner just four days earlier following an extensive refit.

Initial reports suggest an engine failure sparked a fire in the seals before water began pouring into the yacht.

The blaze was quickly extinguished, but the suspected failure may have caused the vessel to lose buoyancy as water flooded in.

However, the exact chain of events behind the dramatic sinking has yet to be officially established.

Fourteen guests and crew were aboard when disaster struck.

Twelve were rescued by a nearby vessel, while the owner and a friend remained aboard the stricken yacht awaiting help.



A La Maddalena Coast Guard patrol boat eventually arrived and took the pair to safety in Poltu Quatu.

Remarkably, no injuries were reported.

The luxury Amer F100 is nearly 30m long and boasted room for up to ten guests across five lavish cabins.



After the rescue, the stricken yacht was secured on the seabed to stop it sinking any further.

Containment booms have also been deployed around the wreck as authorities race to prevent an environmental disaster.

Initial checks found no fuel leaking into the sea.

A huge recovery operation is now being planned, with a pontoon weighing around 200 tonnes reportedly set to haul the wreck from the seabed.

The La Maddalena Port Authority is also preparing measures to force the area to be restored and prevent further environmental damage.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The shock sinking is now under investigation by the Coast Guard, which will attempt to piece together exactly what happened aboard the newly delivered superyacht.

Investigators are yet to establish whether the engine failure triggered the fire, whether the blaze caused the water ingress, or precisely how the yacht ultimately lost buoyancy.

News.title: Huge explosion rocks port in Rotterdam killing at least one and injuring several others during ‘work on pipelines’
News.content:
AT least one person has been killed after a massive explosion rocked Europe’s largest port.

Several others were wounded in the blast at the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands, which occurred while a maintenance crew were working on the pipelines.



Six ambulances, a trauma helicopter and fire crews rushed to the scene in Europoort – a massive, heavily industrialised petrochemical section of the Port of Rotterdam.

The cause of the blast is still unclear and is currently being investigated, a spokesperson for the Rotterdam Police said.



They added that there is no immediate indication that it was caused intentionally, but it is among several scenarios under consideration.

It has been suggested that something may have gone wrong during the disconnection of those pipelines.

“We are cooperating with local authorities,” they added.

Pictures circulated on social media showed visible traces of the explosion on a storage tank.



“An explosion took place on the Moezelweg around 11.30am, a statement from the police said. “We are investigating how this happened.

“A crime scene has been established and the labor inspectorate is also arriving on site. Several people were injured in the explosion and one person has died.“

The incident, which happened around 11.30am, came two hours after emergency crews were also deployed to another major incident in the port.



A Grip 2 emergency, the second level of a crisis management protocol used in the Netherlands, was declared at a refinery on Botlekweg due to a power outage.

The facility has since halted production as a precaution.

The Port of Rotterdam is home to a number of oil and gas companies, so fire crews were standing by.

It is the largest seaport in Europe and the 11th busiest in the world by cargo tonnage.

News.title: How fake pregnancy spiralled into horror newborn kidnap plot after desperate mum-to-be suffers 3 traumatic miscarriages
News.content:
ON THEIR wedding day, they danced joyously to “their special song”, Unchained Melody, as family and friends cheered them on.

Nine years later, Eleonor Alejandra Mendoza and her husband Arturo, unexpectedly heard it played again, but his time while they were in the back of a police car after having been arrested for the kidnapping of a baby.



The extraordinary story of how a young Mexican woman felt such pressure to give birth in a country where family is everything, that she concocted an elaborate plan to fake her pregnancy, is told in the Netflix documentary A Child of My Own.

What starts as an elaborate lie turned into a complex charade that threatened to upend her life and relationship, and ultimately unleashed a media scandal that shook the country.



“I was drawn into problems that got bigger and bigger,” says Ale.

“And I started making decisions and taking actions which got more complicated, until there was no way out. No turning back.”



The documentary is told in an imaginative way by Oscar-nominated director, Maite Alberdi, in which the first half plays out like a drama with actors in the roles of the principal characters in an extended flashback, while the second half features interviews with Alejandra and Arturo, explaining their actions first-hand.

The pair married in July 2000 when Eleonor, known as Ale, was just 17.



“I was pregnant and that’s part of the reason we got married then but I also loved Arturo,” she says.

“I always dreamed of being a mum and I was full of hope.

“I have a large family. All my cousins are mums. I felt like it was fulfilling my dream by having a family of my own.

“When I got married, I felt pressured to please Arturo’s family. I didn’t feel accepted by his mum and that made me want to do everything I could to win her over.”

Ale was devasted when she miscarried while living with her in-laws and felt the “blame” lying heavily on her shoulders.



“I was crying in my bedroom, not wanting to see anyone but they came up to my room.

“One of Arturo’s aunts said, ‘Why are you crying? We all go through this.’ Then his mum said, ‘You should have been more careful. You can’t behave like that.’”

While family continued to talk about them having kids soon, Ale felt the pressure increasing.



“Soon after that first miscarriage, I was pregnant again.

“Arturo would tell me, ‘You have to be careful. Don’t do this, don’t do that.’

“Then I had a second miscarriage. After a few years we started to worry when I didn’t get pregnant.”

Following fertility treatment, she fell pregnant again in 2009, but while working at The General Hospital in Mexico City as an administrative assistant, she had another miscarriage.

It was then, she says, that she met a young woman called Mayra Navarro Vega who was there because she wanted to have an abortion.



“Mayra told me she already had a baby girl from a different father and that her mum would kick her out of the home if she had another.

“She also said the father wasn’t accepting any responsibility, because he didn’t believe the baby wasn’t his.

“Then she said, ‘I’d rather give it away than throw it away.’ I asked her if she was serious, and she said, ‘Yes.’”

The pair then agreed an audacious deal to secretly give the baby to Ale.

“When I got home, I decided I wouldn’t tell anyone that I had lost the baby, especially not Arturo. I didn’t want anyone saying it was my fault, again.”



Instead, she began eating lots of calorific food to put on “pregnancy weight” month by month, going from 119 pounds to 143, 176, all the way to 216.

“My tummy really looked like I was pregnant and I felt so special because people close to you start treating you so lovingly and come up and touch your belly so sweetly.”

Mayra told her that the due date was the week of 16 June, and that the doctors thought it was a girl.

While working in the hospital, Ale looked at the ultrasound Mayra had of her baby and brought a picture of it home to show the family.

Arturo was happy, even though he wanted a baby boy.



When his mum told Ale that she didn’t look like she was carrying a girl, Ale replied that doctors should know better than old wives’ tales of being able to tell the sex from the shape of a woman’s belly.

On a shopping trip with Arturo to buy maternity clothes, she mentioned a baby that her friend was adopting and became upset when Arturo said that he could never adopt because it’s not the same as flesh and blood.

Ale tried to put on a happy face at a baby shower for family and friends but she was feeling the strain of her lie.

“It was awful, seeing everybody happy, my parents, my family, my grandma. I wanted someone to burst that balloon of lies. To spill everything out.”

It was when she was unable to stop Arturo from accompanying her to a doctor for a medical in order to get her maternity leave, that she thought the truth would be revealed.



As Arturo sat in the room, she told the doctor that she was 38 weeks gone.

Then came the moment she was dreading, as he listened to the baby’s heartbeat but couldn’t hear one.

Thinking it was the fault of the device he was using, the doctor went and got an old-fashioned type, and this time, to her disbelief, he said he could hear the baby.

“The doctor gave me my 90 days of maternity leave. I was thinking, ‘Am I pregnant? I lost it, didn’t I? Did I get pregnant again?’ Too much was messed up in my head.”

When Mayra gave birth, Ale pretended to the hospital that she was her neighbour and wanted to see her.



In the ward, Mayra had a fever but pointed to the baby and said the deal was still in place.

“I was holding the baby, when around two or three in the afternoon, a man arrived. He turned out to the be the baby’s father and he took the baby from me and held her.”

Ale walked out and returned later, after visiting hours ended, and says that Mayra was getting dressed to leave.

“I said, ‘You can’t leave me here with her. We have to do this right,’ but Mayra replied, “I did my part. Take the baby.”

Ale put the tiny four and a half pounds tot in a shopping bag and walked out of the hospital. This was later found to have been captured on CCTV camera, which is shown in the documentary.



Outside, she was startled by her husband arriving, who asked her what she was doing. Ale got in the car, with the baby still in the bag, and confessed to what she had done.

Stunned, he angrily ordered her out of the car, telling her to give the baby back.

But he eventually relented and she got back in and they booked into a hotel for the night to talk things over.

Here, Arturo asked her what the plan was going to be. She explained, “Mayra was going to be discharged tomorrow morning. I was going to pretend to be her relative to expediate things.

“By the time you got to the hospital, I’d have the baby, and the paperwork.”



Still angry and shouting, he eventually calmed down enough to hold the baby, telling her, “You’ll be happy with us.”

The three of them fell asleep on the bed, until they were awoken by the police pounding on the door.

They took the baby away and arrested the pair for kidnap, while Ale screamed that the baby had been given to her.

“We were in the police car when on the radio they started playing Unchained Melody, the song we danced to at our wedding,” she recalls.

“It was our special song and, at that moment, I thought, it was a sign. We love each other. We’ll be okay.”



That was Ale’s story and she has stuck by it ever since.

However, Mayra and the baby’s father firmly dispute this and say that their baby, Katya, was simply kidnapped.

A court found Ale guilty of kidnapping and she was given a 13-year prison sentence.

Arturo was locked up for two and a half years until the end of the trial when he was acquitted.

“At the time I felt that Ale had done something unforgivable and that she was evil and I didn’t want to see her again,” says Arturo.



“But being in jail gives you a lot of time to think things over. I reflected on where I might have failed as a partner.

“When I said, ‘I don’t want to adopt, I want a child of my flesh and blood,’ maybe I contributed to closing myself off in that way.

“I admit I did push her a bit, because I wanted to be a dad and I wanted to have a son.”

Once released, he started writing to his wife in prison saying that he forgave her and that he loved her with all his heart.

In the documentary, Mayra gives her side of the story.



“There was never a deal,” she says.

“I didn’t meet her until Katya was born. I only went to the hospital to give birth.

“I had my pregnancy check-ups in another health facility, so I never got to see Ale any earlier.”

Documents confirmed this.

Mayra had not been at the hospital until a few weeks before she gave birth.



“When I was in the hospital, Ale wandered over and showed me her hospital ID badge and said she was doing a survey and she asked me questions like, Was this my first baby? Was she from the same marriage? How was my relationship with her dad?

“That’s where she got all the information.”

Ale denies this but a folder with surveys inside was found beside her jumper and ID badge at the hospital.

There is also footage taken by Katya’s father on his phone, of him tenderly holding his new-born daughter in hospital and talking sweetly to her.

“I had a fever of almost 104F,” says Mayra.



“I couldn’t be discharged because I had an infection. I was asked for urine samples so I left the room and when I returned, my baby was gone.

“My first thought was that maybe a nurse had taken her for a bath or to feed her.

“I never thought she had been stolen.”

The documentary shows Ale being released from prison, having served her sentence, and being reunited with Arturo, who tells her, “It’s over, my love.”

But in a further twist, his yearning to have a son, caused them to part – temporarily.



“Soon after leaving prison, Arturo told me he still wanted to be a dad,” explains Ale.

“I replied that he had the right to pursue his happiness but that I wasn’t willing to undergo any treatment, and with me, he wasn’t going to be a dad.

“We were separated for a while, we gave each other space, and he had a short relationship with another woman and a son was born.

“After that, Arturo came back looking for me.

“We talked and he told me what had happened.



“He said that he missed me, that he loved me, and that he wanted me in his life.

“He asked me to try again and I decided to do so.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It makes me happy to see him fulfilled as a father.

“But even more, it makes me happy that he sees me in his life as the other parent figure of his child.”

News.title: 'Bacteria warning' as beauty item recall issued from B&M and Savers
News.content:
'Bacteria warning' as beauty item recall issued from B&M and Savers

People have been told 'stop immediately' if using this on their face and return it

View 3 Images The product has been recalled as a precaution over 'the possible presence of bacteria which has the potential to cause eye inflammation' (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

People have been told not to use a popular beauty product sold in stores like B&M and Savers. It has been recalled by the manufacturer due to concerns that it may cause "eye inflammation".

‌



Because this is a manufacturer-led product recall initiated by Unilever (Simple's parent company), all stores selling the product are pulling the affected stock. High-street chains like Boots and Superdrug do sell smaller sizes (such as 200ml or 400ml), which are unaffected by this recall.

‌



The company said: "In the UK, we are recalling a limited number of Simple Kind to Skin Micellar Cleansing Water (730ml) products with specific batch codes (613841 or 613941) as a precaution due to the possible presence of bacteria, which has the potential to cause eye inflammation for some consumers. "

‌



The recall is being labelled as "a precautionary measure". The company added: "The safety of the people who buy and use our products is our top priority. Other Simple products are not affected by this issue."

Simple added to the product recall: "If you have any concerns about your health, we recommend seeking advice from a medical professional."

View 3 Images Certain batches of Simple's Kind to Skin Micellar Cleansing Water (730ml) have been recalled (Image: Simple/Unilever)

‌



How do I know if my product is affected?

Check the batch codes listed above to see whether the specific bottle is part of the recall. The batch code can be found at the bottom of the bottle, as a series of numbers printed directly on the packaging.

What should I do if I have a bottle?

The most important thing shoppers should do is avoid using the product. If it matches the recall batch, it should be returned for a refund.

On B&M's website, the recall notice said: "Any customer who has purchased the product is advised to retain the packaging and return the product to a B&M store, where you will receive a full refund. If you have any questions, please contact Customer Services (0330 8389000)."

‌



View 3 Images Savers said people should 'stop using the product immediately' (Image: Getty)

Savers said: "If you have purchased an affected Simple product with one of the batch codes listed above, please stop using the product immediately and contact the Unilever careline by either email or phone for further guidance and a refund.

"The best way to contact Unilever is via email: ukicare@unilever.com. Alternatively, call 0800 146 252 or visit a Savers store with proof of purchase, and we can offer a refund or an exchange."

Article continues below

You do not need to go back to the specific shop where you bought it or still have the receipt to resolve this. Contact Unilever directly by email ukicare@unilever.com with a photo of the bottle showing one of the affected batch codes (613841 or 613941) on the bottom.

News.title: Escaped snake spotted on the loose in Glasgow city centre biting shoppers
News.content:
Escaped snake spotted on the loose in Glasgow city centre biting shoppers

A bright orange snake was spotted on busy Argyle Street, located outside one of the St Enoch Shopping Centre entrances in Glasgow

Moment snake lunges at pedestrians in Glasgow city centre

A snake has been spotted trying to bite shoppers in Glasgow city centre, with people left "raging".

‌



The bright orange reptile was seen crawling on one of the city's busiest shopping thoroughfares, Argyle Street, located outside one of the St Enoch Shopping Centre entrances. The snake was captured in a TikTok video lunging at people's ankles as they walked by.

‌



Other pictures shared online show the snake covered by a cardboard box as a security guard stands near it. The reptile is understood to have been placed in the box to be handed to staff at the shopping centre, the Daily Record reports.

‌



View 2 Images An escaped snake tried to bite shoppers in Glasgow (Image: TikTok/@mcbainthepain)

Golden retriever defies vets to survive FIVE surgeries after he's bitten by a snake READ MORE :

Couple buy cute house in small town but then realise they aren't alone READ MORE :

The animal was eventually collected by the Scottish SPCA and taken to SSPCA's Glasgow Animal Rescue and Rehoming Centre in Cardonald. It remains unclear how the snake ended up in the city centre.

‌



Writing online, one witness said: "The snake was clearly f*****g terrified and could have hurt someone." Others took to social media to share their concern.

Another said: "I know I have an irrational fear of snakes but I always control it by knowing that it is highly unlikely I’d ever come across one randomly …now this!! I was genuinely in town today."

View 2 Images The bright orange reptile was eventually captured by the Scottish SPCA (Image: TikTok/@mcbainthepain)

Article continues below

A third said: "This has made me so raging. The wee soul is in fight or flight. I’d have phoned SSPCA."

An SSPCA spokesperson said: "I can confirm that an Animal Rescue Officer from the Scottish SPCA attended and collected the snake after a member of the public handed it into security at St Enoch Shopping Centre in Glasgow on August 12.

"It was then taken to our Glasgow Animal Rescue and Rehoming Centre in Cardonald where it is now being cared for by the team."

News.title: 'Bomb' found on German train track as police swarm area and evacuation launched
News.content:
'Bomb' found on German train track as police swarm area and evacuation launched

Buildings have been evacuated and the public warned to stay away after a suspected explosive device was found on tracks near Treuchtlingen railway station in Bavaria

View Image German police have been scrambled (file photo) (Image: Getty Images)

Bomb disposal experts have been called in after a suspected explosive device was found on German train tracks.

‌



The area has been cordoned off and members of the public have been urged to stay away from the line as nearby buildings were evacuated by authorities.

‌



This latest alarm comes just days after an explosive-laden drone caused chaos at a German airport after it was found close to a Ukrainian cargo plane.

‌



Police have urged Germans to avoid Treuchtlingen railway station while they inspect the suspicious device. Police said on X: "Currently, as a precautionary measure, some directly affected buildings are being evacuated by emergency response teams.

"The suspicion that it is a potentially explosive device has not yet been ruled out."

‌



Trains passing through the south German town of Treuchtlingen, around 90 miles northwest of Munich, have been suspended while the object is lifted for inspection and X-ray images of the suspicious item are analysed.

German authorities have been on the lookout since a suspected Russian drone carrying a detonator and explosives was found close to a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

The airport was forced to close its runways after the device was found close to a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. Bomb disposal experts were called in after airport workers found the drone.

Article continues below

Experts found a mass, which was identified as explosive material, containing a detonator. The explosive was defective, however, so the bomb did not go off, Bild reports.

Four Ukrainian aircraft were said to be in the immediate vicinity of the drone bomb. Germany’s Interior Minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the drone’s explosive cargo points towards it being a failed attack potentially from “foreign powers”.

There have been a string of unauthorised drone flights in recent weeks at sites across Germany including military installations, seaports, logistics hubs and energy infrastructure - with airports placed on high alert.

News.title: This 'life-changing' holiday supplement is the easy way to keep uncomfortable travel tummy in check
News.content:
This 'life-changing' holiday supplement is the easy way to keep uncomfortable travel tummy in check

Holidays can cause havoc on your bowel movements, but this new supplement pack promises to keep you regular while you’re travelling, so you can concentrate on nicer things

View 4 Images How to have more time having fun and less time in the loo when you're on holiday (Image: Getty / Panama7)

There are so many things to love about holidays. The out-of-office going on, no 9am meeting, sitting by the pool while a tanned waiter brings you a cocktail… it’s heavenly.

But if we’re being terribly picky there is something that can bring a slight dampener to the proceedings. Because the change in routine that holidays bring about can be really tough on your digestive system, causing stomach pain, discomfort, feeling tired or bloated and generally having to spend a lot more time in foreign loos that you would ideally like to.

It's not something we love talking about, but if you have found yourself feeling a bit too blocked up while you're away, this easy course of travel supplements could be the answer to you WC prayers.

View 4 Images We Are. Regular's seven-day pack is ideal for short breaks and travel (Image: We Are. Regular)





Rather than treating holiday constipation with harsh laxatives, which can lead to the sudden, urgent need to find a loo (again, not ideal when you're travelling), We Are. Regular Bowel & Bloat Perfect Poo Starter Pack, £15 is blend of vitamin, minerals and natural botanicals that support digestion, calm bloating and generally help to get things moving. It comes in a seven-day pack - you just mix a sachet with water about half an hour before breakfast each morning. And the satisfaction rates are high.

"Life changing!" says one customer. "After years of struggling, bloating and feeling sluggish and uncomfortable I feel like I’m floating."

"A magic product. I’m one week in, and while I’m not going *every* day, I’ve had more successful and satisfying (seriously satisfying) trips to the bathroom in that one week than I’ve had in the last two months. It is so easy to make, tastes yum, and I am delighted that it doesn’t act as a laxative (I was worried I’d be instantly running to the bathroom)," says another.

"For me, not only has regularity been achieved, but I feel lightly energised throughout the day," says another. It's actually hard to find negative reviews for the product anywhere. Among dozens of happy customers we only found one who didn't like the taste and one who said they'd seen no results over the seven day course.

The star ingredient in We Are. Regular Bowel & Bloat Perfect Poo Starter Pack, £15 magnesium citrate, which draws water back to your bowels. And it's so effective that 79% of testers found they saw results within 24 hours - and 100% by the end of the seven days.

View 4 Images Banish painful tummy troubles in as little as a day (Image: Getty)

Why is toilet trouble so common on holidays?

There's a host of reasons why your digestive system doesn't perform on tip top condition when you go away.

A change in routine

Your bowels love routine, and it's much easier to get that in normal daily life. You probably have a time and place most days where you go to the loo. But when you're away there's a lot that can interrupt that. You might be in a different time zone - even just an hour or two can throw off your body clock. Couple that with early alarms, late dinners, having to wait to find a loo on travel days (that moment where the captain switches on the Fasten Seatbelts sign just as you'd steeled yourself to brave the plane toilet).

Flying

Talking of planes, they are also not friendly to your bowels. You're kept in the same stationary position for hours, and cabin air is dehydrating, pulling water away from your colon to send it to your vital organs instead. The result? Stubborn stools when you land.

Holiday stress

As lovely and relaxing as holidays are, they come with anxieties, too, especially on travel days. 4am alarm call? Did you remember to pack your favourite shorts? Have we got enough time to clear passport control? How do you say 'No I don't want to buy a rose, thank you, please stop asking me'? Anything that's turning your stomach in knots is also affecting your digestion and adding the the problem.

Lovely holiday food

More routine changes - holiday food is often more treat-laden and lower in fibre that our at-home diet. It can also include richer foods, sometimes that your digestive system is less familiar with, and we'll often pack in heavy meals late in the evening.

News.title: A level results day: Grade boundaries for AQA, OCR, Edexcel revealed
News.content:
A record number of students have gotten into university or college (stock)

UCAS figures show the most popular courses are engineering and technology, social sciences and law, with an increase in students getting accepted onto their firm choice

Students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland received their A-Level, BTEC and T-level results this morning - with a record high 262,820 18-year-old accepted onto courses at universities and colleges.

Figures show a significant gap between the proportion of A-level entries in London getting the top grades compared to the north-east or the East Midlands.

Some 32.7 per cent of entries in the capital were awarded A or A* this year, up from 32.1 per cent in 2025 and the highest for any region in England. The North East and the East Midlands had the joint lowest rate, at 23.1 per cent.

The proportion of A-level entries awarded top grades rose for the third year in a row, likely driven by the popularity of maths and students scoring highly in it.

More than a quarter (28.5%) of UK entries were awarded an A or A* grade, up by 0.2% percentage points on last year, when 28.3% achieved the top grades. Maths remained the most popular subject at A-level this year – the 13th year in a row it has topped the table.
