News.title: Brit mum died in Turkey after being 'offered cut-price BBL surgery 10 minutes before op'
News.content:
Brit mum died in Turkey after being 'offered cut-price BBL surgery 10 minutes before op'

An inquest was today told Hayley Dowell had travelled to Istanbul for a tummy tuck and liposuction but was offered a cut-price Brazilian butt-lift just minutes before surgery

View 5 Images A preliminary hearing was told Hayley Dowell suffered an embolism after undergoing surgery at the BHT Clinic in Istanbul (Image: Facebook)

A British mother died after she was offered a cut-price Brazilian butt-lift in Turkey just 10 minutes before going under the knife, an inquest heard today.

‌



Hayley Dowell, 38, had only visited the clinic in Istanbul to undergo treatment for liposuction and to have a tummy tuck. But minutes before her surgery was due, she was made a last-minute offer from her surgeon for the BBL procedure to enhance her "flat" bottom, it was said.

‌



Her husband, Neil Dowell, today told her inquest that he did not think she had signed a consent form to undergo the BBL prior to her operation. It was heard that the surgeon told Mrs Dowell he could take the fat he was removing during the liposuction and use it to enhance her bottom.

‌



View 5 Images Hayley Dowell went under the knife and had a Brazilian butt-lift [BBL], a tummy tuck, and liposuction in October 2023 (Image: FACEBOOK)

Mum who spent life savings on lipo and breast augmentation dies during operation READ MORE :

The inquest heard she was given five minutes to consider the BBL proposal and the surgeon knocked off £1,000. Pathologists believed Mrs Dowell died from a fat embolism from the liposuction, the inquest at Winchester Coroner's Court, Hants, heard.

Mr Dowell, said that she wanted to have a tummy tuck and 360 liposuction because she had three children and was "very self-conscious of her body". Giving evidence at the inquest, he said: "After three children she wanted a flat stomach, and she was always concerned about the weight, so she wanted to trim herself down a bit."

‌



He described her as a "healthy" and "energetic" person, but she did suffer from asthma. When he was asked why Mrs Dowell, from Eastleigh, Hants., decided to go abroad for the surgery, he said: "I think it was more of a trend and obviously the finance situation.

View 5 Images Hayley is said to have paid more than £7,000 for the procedures at the BHT Clinic in Istanbul on October 2 2023

"I think so many people do it and it was something Hayley wanted to do. Friends of hers had done it and had told stories about certain procedures, and she just went for it."

‌



He said that he did not think it was a good idea for Mrs Dowell to have the surgery in Turkey, but she was "very persistent" and had wanted to go for four to five years prior. He said: "I didn't trust it abroad, I thought it should have been the UK, but she was very persistent. "She wanted that procedure, and she had done her research. She looked at the surgeon in Turkey, and that was good enough for her."

The mother of three had the BBL, a tummy tuck, and liposuction - a package that costs more than £7,000 - after the couple arrived in Turkey on October 1, 2023. She went under the knife at the BHT Clinic in Istanbul on October 2 and died "at around midnight" on October 3.

View 5 Images The mum-of-three had a BBL, a tummy tuck, and liposuction (Image: FACEBOOK)

‌



Mrs Dowell had already undergone two breast augmentations in the UK prior to flying to Turkey, and she was curious about having further surgery. Mr Dowell said that Mrs Dowell found Qunomedical online, who asked for images of Mrs Dowell's body, and then they matched her up with a clinic and surgery in Turkey.

He said that Mrs Dowell had persuaded him to have teeth dentures put in while they were in Turkey. He said that they arrived from the airport and they went to an office to sign a consent for the liposuction and tummy tuck, and blood tests were undertaken.

He said that he did not think she was given the consent form to look at overnight and she only looked at it for around 15 minutes. Mr Dowell said that the next day they were both collected at around 6am and taken to the clinic prior to the surgery.

‌



Mr Dowell said he left at around 10am to get his teeth prepared for the dentures, and then he arrived back at around 2pm before Mrs Dowell's surgery. He said about 10 minutes before Mrs Dowell was due to have her surgery, the surgeon came to talk to them and asked if she wanted him to put some of the fat taken out into her bottom because "it was a little flat".

View 5 Images The inquest heard Hayley was made a last-minute offer from her surgeon for the BBL procedure (Image: FACEBOOK)

Mr Dowell said that he thought the surgeon was offering the procedure "off his own back", but then a young woman came round with a card reader to ask for the money. He said they were given a five-minute window to decide on having the BBL procedure.

‌



He said: "She was very embarrassed of her body. We just assumed he was going to use fat from the lipo. She was excited about it. They deducted £1,000 from the procedure because she was already having the other procedure.

"We had five minutes to decide that. We are trying to sort it out. Checking our banks, saying you pay half and I will pay half. It was so quick. We had to make a quick decision. She was going down in 10 minutes after the woman left with the card machine.

"The surgeon never came back in. They came in with anaesthetic to make her a bit drowsy, and they took her away." He said that the BBL should have cost £2,500, but they offered to reduce the price to £1,500, which they agreed to and paid for half each.

‌



Mr Dowell said that he never saw Mrs Dowell sign a consent form for the BBL procedure and he said that doctors at the Turkish clinic did not outline the risks of the procedure to his wife. He said that the doctor had signed the BBL consent form in the morning, but Mrs Dowell had only agreed to the BBL surgery at around 3pm in the afternoon.

Area Coroner for Hampshire, Portsmouth and Southampton, Nicholas Walker said that Mr Dowell was told four hours into the surgery that it was going well. He said that just before midnight, Mr Dowell was told to go with the medical staff because Mrs Dowell was very "unwell" and had suffered two cardiac arrests.

He was told to say his goodbyes, and she died just after midnight on October 3. Mr Dowell then went to the police station and reported the incident. Mr Walker said that Mrs Dowell suffered a fat embolism - an issue that can arise after surgery and causes a potentially fatal blood flow blockage.

‌



He said that the pathologist's evidence carried out in Turkey and agreed as likely in the UK said that she died from micro fat embolism, which affected her lungs, from the liposuction operation.

He indicated he was looking to produce a prevention of future deaths report. Dr Sophie Chung, CEO of Qunomedical, said they were the "facilitators" of the surgery. She said that they no longer worked with the BHT Clinic and they no longer offer BBL surgeries through their company.

She was asked why the surgeon, Dr Salih Basat, was still listed on the company's website, and she said she was not aware, but it was likely that he had changed clinics. The BHT Clinic declined to give evidence at the inquest.

‌



Mrs Dowell is thought to be one of six Britons who died in Turkey in 2023 following medical procedures that went wrong. The country is popular with Britons for its reduced prices on cosmetic surgery, although it has been the subject of warnings by UK health officials.

A BBL involves increasing the size and shape of a person's bottom by removing fat from one area of the body and transferring it to their buttocks.

Last year the UK Government announced a major crackdown on "wild west" cowboys after the Mirror launched a campaign. The then-Health Secretary Wes Streeting vowed to introduce a raft of new laws to deal with dodgy cosmetic surgery in the UK.

Article continues below

The inquest continues.

News.title: Heat exhaustion vs sunstroke: GP explains key warning signs and when to call 999
News.content:
Heat exhaustion vs sunstroke: GP explains key warning signs and when to call 999

As the UK swelters in the heatwave, a GP explains the key differences between heat exhaustion and sunstroke symptoms - and when you need to call 999

View 3 Images Many people are struggling to stay cool in this weather (Image: SimpleImages via Getty Images)

According to the NHS, heatstroke is more serious than heat exhaustion, which can often improve with rest, cooling down and drinking fluids.

‌



Heatstroke is a medical emergency that occurs when the body becomes dangerously overheated and is unable to cool itself down. It can happen during periods of extreme heat or following strenuous exercise and, without prompt treatment, can cause severe damage to the brain and other vital organs.

‌



Meanwhile, heat exhaustion occurs when the body becomes overheated and loses too much water and salt, often because of hot weather or strenuous physical activity.

‌



The Met Office has said the UK is on course for its hottest summer on record, with only average conditions needed for the rest of August to beat the record set just last year. Some parts of the country are facing a fifth heatwave of the summer, with amber extreme heat warnings in place for parts of England on Thursday when temperatures could hit 38C in some spots.

Claire Nevinson, a pharmacist at Boots shared what happens to your body in hot weather, she said: “Our body constantly regulates itself at a core temperature of around 37°C.

"As the surrounding temperature rises, the body tries to cool itself through increasing blood flow to the skin and through sweating. Its this sweating that causes our body to lose water, but if this lost water isn't replaced, the drop in fluid volume can quickly affect your energy levels, concentration and overall wellbeing – sometimes leading to heat exhaustion or heatstroke.”

‌



Claire recommended staying hydrated throughout the day can prevent the risk of heat exhaustion, reports the Express.

View 3 Images Staying hydrated is important during warmer temperatures (Image: fcafotodigital via Getty Images)

She said: “Early signs of dehydration include a dry mouth or lips, thirst, headaches, dizziness, tiredness and dark yellow, strong-smelling urine. However, it's important to note that symptoms vary by age.

‌



“Severe symptoms like confusion, continuous dizziness when standing, seizures, or loss of consciousness require urgent medical help by calling 999 or going to A&E.”

Dr Angela Rai, GP at The London General Practice, spoke to Express.co.uk about heat exhaustion, sunstroke, and the associated health risks. "Being exposed to too much heat can lead to you feeling generally unwell, lacking in energy and feeling dizzy or sick," said Dr Rai.

This is typically an indication of heat exhaustion, which may also trigger other alarming symptoms. Should you spot any signs of heat exhaustion, it's vital to take the correct steps to stop it developing into sunstroke.

‌



"Sunstroke is the most serious form of heat injury and is a medical emergency," warned Dr Rai.

View 3 Images A symptom to look out for in heat exhaustion is a body temperature of around 38C (Image: Getty)

Heat exhaustion symptoms:

‌



Headaches

Loss of appetite

Nausea

Body temperature about 38°C

Excessive sweating

Pale, clammy skin

Feeling very thirsty

Claire added: “Heat exhaustion occurs when the body overheats and it frequently develops alongside dehydration. While it shares similar warning signs with dehydration, the key differentiator to heat exhaustion is marked by additional physical symptoms – specifically muscle cramps, feeling or being sick, and a high body temperature.

“It more commonly affects vulnerable groups, such as older adults, people with chronic health conditions and those taking certain medications. To help manage and prevent heat exhaustion you should focus on actively cooling the body. This includes taking cool showers or using a damp cloth, eating lighter meals, drinking plenty of fluids and keeping indoor air circulating with fans, air conditioning, or open windows.

‌



“If someone continues to show signs of heat exhaustion despite efforts to cool them down, they are at risk of heatstroke, and you should seek urgent medical help by contacting NHS 111 or calling 999.”

Signs of sunstroke:

Body temperature above 40°C

Fast breathing

Shortness of breath

Feeling unwell after resting and cooling off

Feeling confused

Having a seizure

Loss of consciousness

Not being responsive

‌



Dehydration sets in, resulting in electrolyte imbalances and, in more severe cases, complications with kidney function, cardiac abnormalities and dangerous heart rhythms.

There could even be "damage to brain tissue due to brain haemorrhage or swelling".

If you are uncertain whether you are suffering from heat exhaustion or the early stages of sunstroke, dial 111.

Article continues below

Always follow the guidance of the emergency response team, who may advise you to attend hospital.

News.title: Mike Ashley's Frasers Group buys Harvey Nichols after high street giant's plunge into administration
News.content:
Mike Ashley's Frasers Group buys Harvey Nichols after high street giant's plunge into administration

Sport Direct tycoon Mike Ashley indicated his interest in snapping-up Harvey Nichols last week - now he has announced his Frasers Group has bought the famous department store chain

View 2 Images Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group has bought Harvey Nichols (Image: Getty Images)

Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group has bought Harvey Nichols after the department store chain appointed administrators, the Sports Direct owner has announced.

‌



The billionaire Sport Direct tycoon, who has a long history of buying struggling retailers, indicated his interest in snapping-up Harvey Nichols last week after its current owner put it up for sale.

‌



Bosses at Sports Direct owner Frasers said they will now oversee a turnaround at the historic chain following its administration - which could see it become a “smaller business” in the short-term. The luxury department store has suffered several years of losses.

‌



It comes after an auction process for Harvey Nichols which saw Frasers battle retail rival Next to take control of the brand.

Earlier this week, Harvey Nichols warned in its latest accounts that it would need to “cease trading” within a year if it failed to secure new investment.

View 2 Images Harvey Nichols department store in Knightsbridge (Image: Getty Images)

‌



UK construction company plunges into liquidation with over 100 jobs lost READ MORE :

The deal includes the brand’s estate of six stores in Knightsbridge London, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

Frasers Group’s chief executive Michael Murray said: “Harvey Nichols is an iconic British institution with significant potential, but it is clear meaningful change is needed.

“The turnaround will require tough choices and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long-term.”

‌



Speaking to the Financial Times last week, Mr Ashley said he would be inclined to keep the retailer’s flagship store in London’s Knightsbridge and its store in Edinburgh trading under the Harvey Nichols brand.

However, he said some of its other stores would be rebranded as either House of Fraser or Flannels, both of which are owned by Frasers.

There were about 60 House of Fraser stores when Mr Ashley bought House of Fraser for £90million in 2018, whereas there are now just 20.

Article continues below

“These department store buildings are so expensive to maintain,” Mr Ashley told the FT. “ If even John Lewis is struggling, it shows how tough it is. I don’t buy things to close them down. I don’t lose money for no reason.”

Another part of his empire is Lillywhites, the historic sports store on London’s Piccadilly Circus, which he bought for £11.5million in 2002.

News.title: Water bills set to rise for many after firms permitted extra funding
News.content:
Water companies have been given the green light to increase bills for customers by an extra Â£3.4bn in coming years to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.

Nearly a third of the extra funding provisionally approved for 13 water companies in England and Wales is earmarked for making sure water services are maintained.

Some of the rest will be used to meet rising demand from housebuilding and data centres and to address pollutants known as "forever chemicals".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the proposal was "real money out of family budgets at a time when they are struggling with the cost of living", and an environmental group described the decision as "an insult".

Customers of five water companies - Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Thames Water, Wessex Water, and South East Water - are facing additional bill rises over the next two years, on top of increases that were already announced in 2024.

The new increases will vary between firms.

Southern, for example, will charge Â£43 extra next year, while South Eastern will only charge Â£1 more in 2029. The increases will only come into effect if they are given final approval later this year.

The other eight water firms identified - Anglian Water, Dwr Cymru Welsh Water, Hafren Dyfrdwy, Northumbrian Water, Wouth West Water, United Utiliites, Yorkshire Water, SES Water - would recover their additional spending through customer bills after 2030.

Many consumers are angry at being asked to pay anything more against a backdrop of interruptions to supply sometimes lasting for days, and rivers, lakes and beaches too polluted to use safely.

But water companies argue that these problems can only be solved by boosting spending to replace pipes, build treatment plants and establish new reservoirs.

Climate change has also increased pressure on the water infrastructure by making heavy rains and heatwaves more frequent.

News.title: Son pays tribute to dad, 102, who died after allegedly being assaulted in pub
News.content:
The son of a 102-year-old great-grandfather who died after allegedly being assaulted at a south Wales pub says he was a "pub character".

Phillip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following the incident at the Crow's Nest pub in the town on 1 August.

Gwent Police confirmed on Thursday that he had since died.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains under investigation.

Ormerod's son, Robert Ormerod, told the Press Association that his dad had been diagnosed with dementia.

News.title: The key signs you may have damaged your eyes by looking at the eclipse
News.content:
Eye experts are warning people to be on the alert for any signs their vision has been damaged by looking at the sun during Wednesday's eclipse.

The symptoms can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot and increased sensitivity to light.

After the previous total eclipse of the sun that was visible in the UK in 1999, around 70 people were left with damaged sight.

Many of them had spent less than a minute looking at the spectacle, without realising they were harming their eyes.

The danger comes because staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

The sun is incredibly bright, even when partially obscured by the moon.

Normally if we stare at it, we wince and quickly look away.

But when it is darker, during an eclipse, that instinct may not kick in, even while our eyes are being damaged.

The bright light and ultraviolet radiation given off by the sun can lead to a condition known as "solar retinopathy".

And because the retina has no pain receptors, it's hard for people to notice the damage as it happens, so symptoms may only appear several hours later.

Leading up to the eclipse itself, experts were warning only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

News.title: Watch: Key moments from Karoline Leavitt's White House tenure as Trump says she will leave post
News.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her role at the end of August to spend time with her young children and family, after welcoming her second child in May.

"Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," President Donald Trump wrote in a social media post announcing her departure.

Leavitt became the youngest press secretary in the country's history when she took the job in January 2025 at age 27.

News.title: Harvey Nichols bought by owner of Sports Direct
News.content:
Luxury department store Harvey Nichols has been bought by the owner of Sports Direct, which warned a "significant restructuring" was needed to ensure the 200-year-old business remains sustainable.

Mike Ashley's Frasers Group will take control of the Harvey Nichols stores, including its flagship in Knightsbridge, as well as the international franchise.

The department store was immortalised in BBC sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, but had faced challenges in recent years. The firm had appointed administrators in June.

Michael Murray, Frasers' chief executive and Ashley's son-in-law, called the store a "British institution with significant potential" but added "clear meaningful change is needed".

"The turnaround will require tough choices and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long-term," he said.

Harvey Nichols carries more than 800 premium and luxury brands and has over 1,000 employees. Its other stores are located in Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

Frasers Group will also acquire the online business, and shops will continue to operate under their existing licensing.

Earlier this week, Harvey Nichols warned in its latest accounts that it would need to "cease trading" within a year if it failed to secure new investment.

It had faced "sustained trading and operational challenges" recently and Frasers Group said it will need to conduct a review of the store's portfolio, structure and cost base.

A recent auction for the store saw Frasers battle retail rival Next to take control of the firm.

Harvey Nichols was bought in 1991 by Hong Kong-based businessman Sir Dickson Poon but he put the group up for sale earlier this year.

News.title: Busiest ever period for England's A&Es as extreme heat hits
News.content:
England's A&Es are experiencing their busiest period ever, with the record-breaking heat cited as a key factor.

More than 2.4 million patients attended emergency departments each month for May, June and July â the three highest monthly totals recorded in history.

NHS bosses say the pressure has been as bad as it is in winter months. The extreme heat has caused people to fall ill with dehydration and heatstroke, and has increased the risk of complications for those with heart, kidney and respiratory problems.

It comes as unions warn staff are being forced to work in inhumane conditions because of the heat, with reports of some collapsing and others having seizures.

The problems have been further complicated by equipment, including scanners and IT systems, breaking down.

NHS medical director Prof Frankie Swords praised the "outstanding professionalism" of staff and said the situation was making delivering care challenging.

She advised: "With temperatures peaking today, please take sensible precautions to stay safe - keep hydrated, avoid the sun during the hottest part of the day, especially if you are clinically vulnerable, and check in on older or vulnerable friends, relatives and neighbours."

News.title: Met chief accepts mistakes made over Simon Levy but defends investigation into murders
News.content:
The head of the Metropolitan Police Sir Mark Rowley has defended the force's investigation into double murderer Simon Levy.

Levy was on bail and being monitored by police when he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later, as well as violently raping a third woman.

Sir Mark acknowledged mistakes over the force's handling of Levy, but said suggestions it had not tried to build a case over his first murder were "just not true", following criticism including from Labour MP Jess Phillips.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that detectives had done "serious" work but "didn't have enough evidence" for a charge.

The Met did not seek a charging decision from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) over Valencia-Trujillo's murder until after Wilkins had been killed.

The police and CPS has apologised over a series of decisions that left the convicted sex offender free to attack the women.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is currently examining how Levy, 40, was managed over the four-year period from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, he was given a whole life prison sentence, meaning he will never be released.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark - who on Wednesday called the case a "whole system failing" - said he had already apologised for what the Met had got wrong.

It emerged after Levy's conviction that the Met did not class Valencia-Trujillo's death in March 2025 as a murder, or pass the case to specialist homicide detectives, until after he had killed again.

Sir Mark said "the public debate needs to be better informed" because "the facts on that are much more complex than people want to acknowledge".

He said that while Valencia-Trujillo's death was "clearly very suspicious and concerning", a pathologist was unable to determine a cause of death and the force "didn't have enough evidence to get to a charge".

Sir Mark added it was only after the murder of Wilkins that the Met had the "combined evidence" to move forward.

"So the inference that the Met didn't try on that case is just not true, the Met tried," he said.

However, the Met did not ask the CPS for advice about Valencia-Trujillo's death, let alone a charging decision, until after the murder of Wilkins, the BBC has previously reported.

The fact there was no formal cause of death would not have prevented the case being taken on by specialist homicide detectives, who are skilled at building murder cases even when there is not a formal cause of death.

Levy's semen was on Valencia-Trujillo and his blood was at the murder scene. CCTV that showed Levy in the area, walking in the same direction as Valencia-Trujillo shortly after she passed a camera, was not viewed by the local team despite being gathered.

Other possible relevant CCTV was never gathered, and had been deleted by the time the specialist murder team took over months later.

In that case, the local team investigating the death did not engage with the Met's specialist murder teams apart from the day her body was discovered in March 2025.

A specialist homicide team attended the crime scene that day and recommended the case stay with local officers pending further enquiries, but there was no further contact until after Wilkins was murdered in August.

News.title: Voting under way in Clacton by-election
News.content:
Voting is under way in the Clacton by-election as a record number of candidates vie to become its next MP.

Fifty-one polling stations in the Essex resort, which includes the towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze, opened at 07:00 BST and will shut at 22:00.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: UK economy grows but experts warn of challenging months ahead
News.content:
Summer sun and sports fixtures helped the UK economy grow between April and June, according to official data, but some economists warned the outlook for the rest of the year was weaker.

The economy expanded by 0.4%, in line with market expectations but below a 0.6% increase in the first three months of this year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with the UK ahead of other G7 countries for growth this year so far.

Experts questioned whether this resilience would be maintained, however, given growth was fuelled by some temporary factors and energy prices could remain volatile if the Middle East conflict continues.

The British economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, the ONS said, despite fears that the Iran war, which started at the end of February, and politically uncertainty around Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister would hold back growth.

Between April and June, sectors including computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry lifted growth. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.

The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3%.

The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, increased customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.

June also saw several of summer's heatwaves. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.

News.title: Boy suffered fatal brain injury in seaside drowning
News.content:
A seven-year-old boy suffered a fatal brain injury after he got into difficulty off the Essex coast, a coroner has said.

Musa Ahmed died six days after the incident in West Mersea, in which his 15-year-old cousin, Sameeha Rahman, and her mother, Shelina, 41, also died.

They were all enjoying a day out to the island, near Colchester, from east London when the tragedy unfolded on 22 July.

Their provisional causes of death were all given as drowning at an inquest opening in Chelmsford, while Musa also died from a hypoxic ischaemic brain injury.

"Clearly it is so tragic to come across the death of any individual," said Lincoln Brookes, the senior coroner for Essex.

"But when three occur at the same time and all from the same family, one cannot understand the tragic nature of such an incident."

Three others were taken to hospital by ambulance after the incident and are said to be recovering.

News.title: 'The fish is in the right' says man bitten after catching blue shark
News.content:
The blue shark is a long-distance migrant that is present in Irish waters usually from June to October, when it is taken by recreational anglers on a catch-and-release basis, according to Inland Fisheries Ireland, external.

It says the blue shark is one of Ireland's largest and most valuable marine sport fishes.

Jack Kelly, a marine biologist and cinematographer in County Galway, said they are "common all around Britain and Ireland during the summer months".

"You can definitely get them in numbers," he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster.

Kelly said all sharks are "so curious in an amazing way".

"If a shark approaches anything, really, it's not like they have fingers to be able to investigate to see what it is. So they have this amazing curiosity about them where they'll come, they'll just kind of circle and try to check out what's going on," he said.

"You'll often get them actually just really staring at you.

"For me, when I'm underwater they might give the camera a bump just to see what it is, so their curiosity for me is definitely something that stands out."

Blue sharks can reach more than three metres in length and feed in open water on fish, squid, smaller sharks and sea birds.

The conservation status of the blue shark is listed as near threatened on the Irish Red List for cartilaginous fish and by the IUCN Red List, according to Inland Fisheries Ireland.

The Marine Sportfishing Tagging Programme, external tagged 19,309 blue sharks between 1970 and 2013 off the coast of Ireland, which accounts for 45% of all tagged fish since the beginning of the programme.

This is not the first time people have been bitten by sharks off the Irish coast.

In 2018, a Belfast man who was angling caught a blue shark and was bitten while bringing it on board a boat.

His lower arm was seriously injured in an incident where he was helped by Crosshaven RNLI in Cork.

News.title: XL bully dog which fatally bit man was not type to savage anyone, defendant says
News.content:
A woman who denies owning an XL bully that bit her partner's father, causing him to bleed to death, has told a court the animal was not "the type of dog to savage anyone".

Chanel Fong, 33, is accused of being the owner of the dog, Cookie, that was allegedly dangerously out of control at the time, as well as an alternative charge of being the person in charge of the dog at the time of the attack.

Her partner's father, Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, died from severe blood loss after being bitten on the leg.

The court heard he had been in poor health and had been taking methadone and blood thinning medication, and had been staying at Chanel Fong's Wrexham home in May 2022.

News.title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant failings
News.content:
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.

But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".

There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.

This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.

The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.

The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.

It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.

Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.

News.title: Farm show bans cattle and sheep amid outbreak
News.content:
Some 353 cases of bluetongue serotype 3 (BTV3) have been recorded in the UK in the 2026/27 season - most of them in the south-west of England.

The virus is spread by insects and is generally found in cattle, sheep and goats. It does not affect people or food safety but it causes a high rate of death in infected sheep and fertility problems in infected cattle.

Barrow said the team had been working closely with vets ahead of the show.

"We've worked through lots of different scenarios as to ways that we could keep the cattle and sheep and goat sections going, such as only bringing vaccinated sheep or putting on a really reduced, very local show.

"But, we thought because the situation is ever-changing and the volume of cases was just increasing exponentially, that the best thing for us to do for this year was to withdraw our cattle sheep in eight sections."

"We felt because we have a big cattle and sheep section, that bringing people in from quite far out of area, just wouldn't have been the best thing for us to do while it's still a new and emerging situation, and we're still learning all about it," she added.

Organisers of the Launceston Agricultural Show took the same decision in July regarding cattle and sheep.

News.title: Residents' 'absolute fear' as massive fire destroyed their homes
News.content:
People preparing to watch the eclipse were instead witness to a massive fire that destroyed homes and left 20 people evacuated to a leisure centre, a councillor in south Wales has said.

There are no reports of casualties, but six bungalows were evacuated near Hazelwood Road, Newbridge, in Caerphilly county, on Wednesday.

"Everyone was getting ready yesterday to witness the eclipse, and for this to happen last night was a total shock," said councillor Gary Johnston.

Julia Nichols, 74, was one of the people evacuated from her home in Pantside and said the fire left her in "absolute fear".

News.title: Three teenagers guilty of man's murder and robbery
News.content:
Three teenagers on a violent mission "to obtain money or drugs" have been found guilty of murdering a man.

The body of David Cuthbert, 49, was discovered with stab wounds at a house in Egglescliffe Close, in Stockton, on 10 January.

Layton Lightfoot and Jesse Reaney, both 18, and Charlie Wilcock, 19, were convicted of murder and robbery following a trial at Teesside Crown Court on Wednesday.

Lightfoot, of Stockwith Close in Middlesbrough, Reaney, of Lowthian Road in Hartlepool, and Wilcock, of no fixed address, are due to be sentenced on 27 November.

Det Supt Daryll Tomlinson, of Cleveland Police, said the three defendants were "heavily involved in criminality" and had sought to "assert their authority" and "brazenly brag about their violence to those online".

He said: "[They] were on a mission that day to use violence through the use of weapons to obtain money or drugs from those living within the community."

Blue Bloods alum Jennifer Esposito has opened up about her difficult health journey and the severe depression and panic attacks that led to an “excruciating” stay in a psych ward.

Appearing on a recent episode of the Heal Squad podcast, the 53-year-old — best known for playing Detective Jackie Curatola on the hit CBS show — detailed the myriad of physical and mental health symptoms she experienced as a result of undiagnosed celiac disease.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition in which the consumption of gluten, found in rye, wheat and barley, causes the immune system to overreact and mistakenly attack the small intestine.

Esposito recalled that it was during her two-season stint on the sitcom Samantha Who? when “things started to collapse.”

“I had hair falling out, nails falling off,” she said. “A tooth fell out of my mouth, like literally in the middle of a scene. I was so depressed [about] being so sick all the time, and fighting panic disorder.”

open image in gallery Jennifer Esposito was admitted to a psych ward because of severe depression and panic attacks ( Maria Menounos/YouTube )

open image in gallery Esposito eventually discovered her severe panic disorder was a symptom of undiagnosed celiac disease ( Getty )

Eventually, she went to a female doctor who listened to her entire health history and took blood tests before discovering Esposito had one of the worst cases of celiac disease she had ever seen.

“She’s like, ‘I’m not sure how you’re alive; My liver was failing,” the actor recounted. She explained that her body was taking nutrients from her nervous system, which is why “my panic disorder was out of control.”

“When I stopped the gluten and went through this detox, they had me on four Klonopin a day” as a way to treat her panic attacks, she said.

“I was literally sleeping in my kitchen,” Esposito added, “because it was the only place that didn’t have a window because the stimulus from the light would make me tremble and shake.”

Months after her diagnosis, she connected with a medical expert who wanted to study her “because I was so ill.”

Esposito remembered on one particular visit, pleading with the doctor to keep her there “because I’m jumping out of my skin. I’m going to jump out the window.”

open image in gallery Esposito is best known for playing Detective Jackie Curatola on 'Blue Bloods' ( Getty )

The doctor interpreted her remark as suicidal, “and within half an hour, I was wheeled upstairs to the psych ward,” she said. “I will say it was seven of the most excruciating hours of my entire life because I was yet again pleading for my sanity.

“You can’t put someone who’s having severe panic disorder in a locked space,” she noted, adding that the doctors continued to misunderstand her symptoms.

“And it was because I said I was going to jump out the window, they thought I was going to harm myself,” Esposito continued.

“I remember [the doctor] looked at my dad and he was like, ‘Is she always this hostile?’” she said. “And I just thought, if I ever get out of here … I have to do something.”

Her experience inspired her to share her difficult health journey in her 2014 memoir, Jennifer’s Way, and to connect with other celiacs through community groups.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

Pandora’s CEO says fresh jewelry lineups are driving growth as the retailer diversifies its core business of silver charm bracelets.

"What we are doing in terms of distinctive newness is working, so where we are launching new collections that are inspiring and good for consumers we are delivering growth," CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier said Thursday. She stepped into the top job on January 1 after serving as chief marketing officer.

Pandora shares climbed 4% at the market open after the group raised its 2026 profit outlook on the back of U.S. tariff refunds, while posting stronger than anticipated second-quarter sales.

De Pablos-Barbier’s strategy centers on introducing novel designs with distinct aesthetics and a broader range of metals, moving past the core offer of silver charm bracelets.

Its Pandora Wonders line — featuring pearl and gold charms shaped as frogs, pufferfish, or mushrooms — debuted in July during Paris Haute Couture week.

open image in gallery ( REUTERS )

The business is transitioning to platinum-plated products to lower silver reliance after price surges last year. De Pablos-Barbier noted yellow-plated gold ranges are a primary growth source as gold jewelry increases in popularity.

Even so, volatile metal costs make Pandora’s profit trajectory hard to predict, Citi analyst Thomas Chauvet noted, despite silver exposure being hedged for 2026.

"Near-term conviction is further limited by an uncertain consumer backdrop in North America and Europe (~85% of sales), as well as execution risk associated with the planned shift to platinum-plated collections," Chauvet added.

European summer heatwaves also weighed on store visits, steering shoppers online, de Pablos-Barbier explained.

"We saw a disproportional increase versus last year on e-commerce, so I think people stayed in their home and decided not to go out on the street," she said.

Though comparable sales across Europe and North America dropped in the second quarter, overall organic growth reached 3% — topping the 2% expected by analysts — primarily driven by store expansions. Weak demand among mid- and lower-income U.S. consumers continued to hamper store traffic, the company noted.

Star Wars and Marvel are officially joining forces for the first time ever with a crossover book series.

A five-issue limited comic book run called Star Wars/Marvel: Hope Assembles will mark the first time that characters from the Marvel Comics universe and Star Wars universe will appear on the page together, Lucasfilm and Marvel announced in a press release Tuesday.

“Marvel and Star Wars’ histories have been intertwined for 50 years and continue to set the standard for storytelling across the world… and across the media landscape,” newly appointed Marvel Comics Editor-in-Chief Stephen Wacker said in a press release. “Lifelong lovers of both Star Wars and Marvel have a lot to look forward to as we finally bring the characters together in ways fans have been dreaming about for decades!”

Star Wars/Marvel: Hope Assembles will follow Marvel heroes like Captain America, Iron Man and the Hulk after a spell shatters reality and brings the Star Wars universe to earth.

“The Avengers, Spider-Man, and more will team up with heroes like Luke Skywalker, Princess Leia, Han Solo, and Chewbacca, while Doctor Doom will align himself with the likes of Darth Vader and the Galactic Empire,” the press release explains.

open image in gallery 'Star Wars/Marvel: Hope Assembles' will be released in 2027 for the 50th anniversary of 'Star Wars: A New Hope' ( Lucasfilm )

open image in gallery Darth Vader and Doctor Doom will fight Marvel and 'Star Wars' characters in the new comic book series ( Lucasfilm )

The new issue — which will be released ahead of the 50th anniversary of Star Wars: A New Hope in 2027 — will be written by comic book superfan and filmmaker Kevin Smith, with art by Marvel comic artist David Marquez.

“Back in the early 80’s, I had a subscription to Marvel’s Star Wars comics,” Smith said in a statement. “And as fun as it was to follow the continuing adventures of Luke, Leia, and Han, I always wished that Spider-Man or Doctor Doom could cross over into their cinematic saga. So when the opportunity arose to actually tell that story, nobody had to Force my hand! I’m ecstatic to be writing Hope Assembles for the 50th anniversary of Star Wars! Many thanks to Marvel Comics and Lucasfilm for trusting me to fly the Falcon and the Quinjet!”

Star Wars and Marvel go way back. The first Star Wars comics were published by Marvel on April 12, 1977, and relaunched in 2015.

Michael Siglain, the creative director of Lucasfilm Publishing, said in the press release: “Now, 50 years later, it's only fitting that the Star Wars galaxy collides with the Marvel universe to celebrate the 50th anniversary of A New Hope.”

He added, “Hope Assembles is exciting, unpredictable, and heartfelt. In short, it's comics at its best, and we can't wait for readers to experience both franchises as never before,” he concluded.

The first issue of the comics will launch in January 2027, with each installment dropping every month until the fifth and final issue is published in May 2027.

News.title: ‘Well-known’ great-grandfather, 102, dies after alleged assault in Welsh pub
News.content:
For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A 102-year-old great-grandfather who died after allegedly being assaulted at a pub was a “well-known character” who locals would buy drinks for, his son said.

Phillip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following the incident at the Crow’s Nest pub in the town on August 1.

Gwent Police confirmed on Thursday that he has since died.

His son, Robert Ormerod, said his father had dementia and lived alone in the Llanyrafon neighbourhood he had raised his family in.

He said his father used to visit the Crow’s Nest regularly and described him as a popular character who young people would buy beer for when he visited the bar.

Mr Ormerod said: “I feel sad – even though he could be difficult because of his age and dementia, still, you get used to him being around.

open image in gallery Phillip Ormerod, aged 102, from Cwmbran ( PA )

“Even though I suppose he wouldn’t go on forever, he would’ve carried on, I think, for a bit.”

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli was arrested on suspicion of section 20 assault and remains under investigation.

open image in gallery Crow’s Nest pub in Cwmbran, Wales ( Google )

Emergency services were called to the pub in Cwmbran, South Wales, at about 10.25pm on 1 August following a report of an assault.

DCI Shelley Comley, senior investigating officer for Gwent Police, said: “We understand the public interest in this incident but want to remind people that not only is this an active criminal investigation but there is a family at the heart of it processing the loss of a loved one.

“Please consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments – particularly online commentary – could have on them and the ongoing investigation as a whole.”

Gwent Police are looking to speak to anyone who was in the pub between 10pm and 11pm on the night of the incident.

Anyone with information can contact the force by calling 101 quoting log reference 2600249432.

Alternatively, Crimestoppers can be contacted anonymously on 0800 555 111 or through their website.

The Federal Trade Commission is sending out more than $23.8 million to Grubhub drivers and diners who the agency says were harmed by the food delivery company’s misleading earnings claims and other deceptive practices.

The agency announced Wednesday that 640,038 people will receive payments by check or PayPal. Affected app users will receive payments automatically without needing to fill out a form. Most recipients will get their payment by mail and should cash the check within 90 days. Those receiving money through PayPal will have 30 days to claim it, the FTC said.

In December 2024, the FTC and Illinois Attorney General jointly filed a lawsuit, along with a proposed $25 million settlement, over allegations that Grubhub used deceptive practices to grow its business.

Grubhub had long promoted a single, low-cost delivery fee, but regulators said it later added extra charges labeled as “service” or “small order” fees, sometimes pushing the final price to more than twice what customers initially saw. One former Grubhub executive reportedly described the pricing strategy as a “pricing shell game,” according to the FTC.

Beginning in at least 2019, Grubhub also allegedly listed restaurants on its platform without having agreements with them. The FTC said the practice made Grubhub’s network appear larger and sometimes resulted in orders being sent to restaurants that had not partnered with the company, creating headaches for both businesses and customers.

Most Grubhub diners and drivers will receive their portion of the settlement in a check sent in the mail, the Federal Trade Comission said Wednesday ( Getty/iStock )

Some customers allegedly lost access to gift card funds after Grubhub locked accounts containing large balances. Customers were sometimes left without a clear explanation or an easy way to regain access to their money, according to the FTC.

Grubhub was accused of overstating how much drivers could earn. In New York City, for example, Grubhub allegedly advertised earnings of up to $40 an hour, even though the median driver earned about $10 an hour. However, just one in 1,000 drivers reached the advertised rate, according to the FTC.

Although Grubhub did not admit to wrongdoing, it agreed to settle the FTC’s case.

At the time of the company’s settlement, Grubhub said in a statement: “At Grubhub, we’re committed to transparency so that every single day diners, restaurants and drivers can make well-informed choices to do business with us. While we categorically deny the allegations made by the FTC, many of which are wrong, misleading or no longer applicable to our business, we believe settling this matter is in the best interest of Grubhub and allows us to move forward.”

Under the settlement, Grubhub agreed to make “substantial changes,” including being more upfront about driver pay, giving users a way to challenge blocked accounts and only listing restaurants that have agreed to be on the platform, the FTC said.

The Independent has contacted Grubhub for comment.

NANTUCKETT, Mass. — It’s 7:45 am. Inside The Landing Cafe, just a few steps from Hyannis Harbor, blonde 20-somethings in Parke sweatshirts carrying identical canvas bags are milling about, eyes glued to their phones, waiting to board the Nantucket ferry.

There’s a rough hour-long ride ahead — the storm clouds portend choppy seas and 47 mph wind gusts. Ironically, I’m heading to the island to find out about a storm of a different kind — one that’s been brewing between social media influencers who use the island as an idyllic backdrop for their content, and locals and second-home owners who have been regulars for years.

In Apple TV’s summer hit Widow's Bay, Tom Loftis, the mayor of the fictional New England island, played by Matthew Rhys, desperately wants to turn the cursed, isolated town into a thriving tourist hotspot like Nantucket. But arguably, Nantucket, where old money and new money have long collided over dock space and dinner reservations, has something more insidious going on: the creeping sense that the very thing that sustains it might also be destroying it.

This all erupted in the past few weeks when John Sylvia, a 59-year-old antiques dealer whose family has sold nautical curios on the island for nearly a century, hung a hand-painted quarterboard from the ceiling of his shop, Four Winds Craft Guild. In gold leaf, it reads: "No Influencers." But when Sylvia’s partner, Jessica Jenkins, 50, who manages the store’s social media, posted a picture of the sign on Instagram, the message quickly blew up.

“Influencers have ruined every place from Kyoto to Paris,” wrote one commenter. “You cannot see anything at an art museum because of the line of people taking multiple selfies and blocking paintings.”

open image in gallery The 'No Influencers' sign on display in John Sylvia’s Nantucket shop Four Winds Craft Guild set off a firestorm of debate on the normally staid island off Cape Cod ( Alex Hannaford/The Independent )

Then, Paige Paul, an influencer who commands over a million followers and recently opened a clothing store, Dairy Boy, on the island, said that given that the influencer orbit is dominated by women, Sylvia’s sign was effectively "barring women.”

“Mocking women when they become powerful in a new industry isn't new,” she posted.

The battle lines were drawn. In her shop, Paul hung up her own sign in response: "Everyone Welcome.”

Nantucket has indeed become ground zero for this very 21st-century collision, the kind playing out in any place where tourism has tipped from economic engine to existential threat. And social media content creators, or influencers, make themselves easy targets — visible, stereotypical in presentation, and invariably young and female.

The “No influencers” sign earned Sylvia a New York Times visit and he told the paper it was meant to be tongue-in-cheek — a joke about visitors who treated his store as a stage, filming without buying anything or even making conversation.

But the comments under the story were more blatant in their condemnation.

“So-called influencers are the scourge of the modern world today,” wrote one.

What happened on Nantucket exposed the fault line between those who see influencers — and by extension modern social media — as a societal irritant, and those who see the hostility toward them as the real elitism.

open image in gallery Influencer Paige Paul, nee Lorenze (pictured at the 2025 US Open in NYC with a Dobel Tequila Ace Paloma cocktail), says of the Nantucket kerfuffle: “Mocking women when they become powerful in a new industry isn't new” ( Getty )

There’s an old saying on Nantucket: tourists come to the island with a dirty shirt and a $5 bill — and don’t change either. Greg Creedon says that’s been the case since the 1960s.

Creedon, 74, moved to Nantucket with his parents when he was four weeks old. His grandfather was superintendent of schools here. A retired tech worker who now works part time handing out tourist pamphlets, he meets me off the ferry and agrees to show me around.

We hop in his pickup truck and immediately hit traffic.

“There are places on the island where it's almost impossible to drive,” he says, and then goes on to describe Nantucket’s “commercial pattern” much as anyone who has seen the Spielberg classic Jaws once or twice might expect.

“You open Memorial Day, you have a slow month in June, then the Fourth of July hits and it’s off to the races until the middle of August,” Creedon tells me. “By then, a lot of people are really cranky. By the time kids start going back to school, the tourists start drifting away and we begin that long trip down into winter.”

Creedon sums up the influencer issue in his own inimitable Nantucket islander way: “Pointless tourism.”

The problem that those who sympathize with Sylvia’s “No Influencers” sign have is that they feel the island has become a destination to be photographed rather than lived; consumed rather than experienced.

They feel that these new, younger visitors, arrive with itineraries built for engagement metrics rather than engagement with the island itself: they clog the ancient cobblestone streets for the perfect selfie, treat century-old shops as backdrops, and leave behind a trail of photographic breadcrumbs for the next wave of the young and Instagram-obsessed to follow

open image in gallery Paul's Dairy Boy shop regularly curates lines outside its Nantucket boutique and is at the center of a social media culture war at the beach getaway ( Alex Hannaford/The Independent )

Creedon describes it as a version of the bucket list — but on steroids. As we approach Dairy Boy, a line of young, mostly women devotees, snakes down the wooden staircase from the front door and along the street. It’s one-in-one-out, and I count 17 people waiting for their chance to peruse the beachwear, pajamas, workout shorts, colorful zip-up fleeces, and Wellington boots inside.

One of them, Hannah Moser, 26, has come with four friends. They’re vacationing on Cape Cod, but have ferried over to Nantucket for a night. “I heard about Dairy Boy on TikTok,” Moser tells me.

Her friend follows Paige Paul’s account, but Moser says the shop also appeared in her feed. Most people, she says, order the clothing online, but as she and her friends were on the island for the day anyway, they decided to check it out in person.

Another woman, a 23-year-old who only gives her first name, Jayne, says she, too, heard about Dairy Boy via TikTok and wanted to see it as she was on the island for a vacation with her family. “I liked the look of the clothes and wanted to see the store. I wouldn’t have come here just for this, but it’s a small town and I pass by every day.”

Inside the shop, it’s not crowded — there are about 12 people looking round — and I wonder whether the one-in-one-out policy is by design, to keep a line always visible, right out of the velvet-rope nightclub playbook.

open image in gallery Greg Creedon, 74, who has lived on Nantucket since he was a baby, calls the scourge of influencers, ‘Pointless tourism’ ( Alex Hannaford/The Independent )

Paul, who married American tennis player Tommy Paul in July but is better known by her maiden name Lorenze, did not respond to The Independent’s request for an interview.

Back outside, Creedon leads me through a door next to the Dairy Boy entrance.

“I'm going to show you one of the funniest incongruous things I've seen in a long time that I'm surprised nobody has pointed out,” he says. “In the office space above Dairy Boy is an organization called Sustainable Nantucket. You can’t make this up.”

The mission of Sustainable Nantucket is to help the island community by supporting local agriculture, food producers and craftspeople. Posie Constable is its managing director, and we sit down at a cluttered table in her office.

According to the 2020 census, Nantucket island has a year-round population of a little over 14,000. In July and August that number swells to around 80,000 or more.

“It’s a huge swing,” Constable says. “And for that reason, locals, while they love the revenue, can’t wait for tourist season to be over so they can reclaim their beaches and restaurants.”

She says it’s one event after another — dance festival, film festival, comedy festival, book festival. Not to mention the weddings. “The chamber of commerce has created all these events and helped create events that bring people here. So we've kind of done it to ourselves a little bit.”

open image in gallery Nantucket is known to attract crowd-drawing events and pop-ups to the island. Here, Martha Stewart attends her Nantucket by Design Dinner on July 15, 2025 ( Getty Images for Nantucket Histo )

open image in gallery ... Meanwhile, shoppers enjoyed the Searchlight Pictures pop-up for "The Roses" at The Boarding House a month later ... ( Getty Images for Searchlight Pic )

open image in gallery ... And the Nantucket Film Festival brings filmmakers and movie lovers in droves. Here, guests attend the 'Toast to the End of NFF' in 2019 ( Getty )

Constable says 52 percent of Nantucket is in conservation — protected from development in perpetuity. But what that means is that for every new house that’s built, or old one torn down and rebuilt, there’s less available land for workforce housing to accommodate the people who keep its economy going.

“Our teachers, our healthcare workers, our town officials,” she rattles off.

Constable jokes that she’s too old to understand why young people are drawn to a culture of capturing everything on their phone — she says her daughters, who are in their 30s, call her a “Karen” when she goes off about having to walk through the scrum on Nantucket’s streets each day.

As for Dairy Boy, her downstairs neighbor, she says she wants to maintain a good relationship with all businesses on the island. Problems start to arise, she says, because of Nantucket’s size.

“[Growth] is more immediately impactful here because of our congested cobblestone streets. This is a very quaint place. And [it’s hard to] maintain the quaintness of our downtown when a merch drop is announced on Instagram, and then two or three truckloads of Cape Cod Express trucks roll up, offload boxes and boxes on pallets, and it all gets dragged back there,” she says.

“I’m not here to judge, but I am exhausted by the sense that this is not Nantucket. It's supporting the tax base, but it's at the expense of others who would like to also claim this as their island with less fanfare.”

Michael Harrison is chief curator at the Nantucket Historical Association, which has conducted extensive research into the island’s tourist economy.

open image in gallery Tommy Paul with Paige Lorenze after his Championships 2024 win in London. The couple wed this summer, and she took his last name ( Getty Images )

Harrison reflects on Nantucket’s history as a whaling port. When the whaling industry collapsed, the islanders, looking for a new economic engine, decided it could become a summer resort destination. This happened just after the Civil War in latter 1800s. “And what the island provides for people who summer here versus what the island provides for the people who live here year-round has been a consistent source of tension since then,” he says.

But what has changed is the scale of that tourist economy. What was once hotel visits is now mostly second or even third homes. “There are day trippers on Nantucket today, but a lot of it is people who stay for a week or a month or have a seasonal home,” Harrison says.

The other thing to understand, he maintains, is that the tourist economy that’s on the island is not one founded on hot dog sales and T-shirts. “The engine of our economy is construction, real estate sales, and all the maintenance and infrastructure that keeps these summer homes going. Food sales and souvenirs and all of that are just a drop in the bucket compared with everything else,” he says.

There are only so many homes available, and so, Harrison says, you see older homes torn down to make way for bigger, more modern abodes. “I want a pool, I want a guest house, I want six more bedrooms,” he says of the newer buyers.

“The construction of all of that — the real estate transactions — that's a big deal, and because there's such competition to acquire those summer homes, the locals can't compete anymore with buying real estate or finding places to rent. That's been a problem for a long time, but it's getting worse and worse.”

open image in gallery Nantucket locals say the influx of influencers and their followers is impinging on the quaint seaside summer experience their little island off Cape Cod is known for ( Alex Hannaford/The Independent )

open image in gallery ... Influencer Paige Paul's Dairy Boy is the epicenter of that battle ( Alex Hannaford/The Independent )

I ask Harrison whether young influencers and young people with smartphones may be just the most visible sign of this tourism explosion right now; that perhaps they’re just an easy target, but that there's much more going on behind the scenes.

“There are those whose families have summered on Nantucket for a hundred years. Then there are the people who think, ‘Oh, Nantucket's the hot place to be. I'm going to go there now and record it for Instagram.” But, he says, there's even a tension there that doesn't involve the year-round community; a tension that gets at who gets to call Nantucket their own.

“Many people I know who have summer homes and come here for three months a year talk like they belong here; that they are Nantucketers in their imagination and they’ve earned it because for 70 summers they've been here,” he says.

“Meanwhile, the locals say, ‘Well you don't winter here.’ So there's always a lot of back and forth. But the locals hate the traffic, and the people who've been here for 70 summers hate the traffic, too. And we all bemoan how expensive everything is getting, and we all think it's a problem that there's there's not enough housing. So I think there are other, deeper systemic issues than whatever this [influencer issue] happens to be right now.”

Still, product lines and film companies and the like love to lure influencers to Nantucket to promote their wares.

My friend Angela Pham, a commercial photographer and content creator based in Upstate New York, recently returned from a press trip to Nantucket, organized by the luxury Italian brand LaDoubleJ. She told me the company had invited 10 fellow influencers but that due to a storm (not just me then) only two made it out there — Pham and another woman.

open image in gallery The 'tongue-in-cheek' sign that launched a class war on Nantucket is displayed in Four Winds Craft Guild ( Alex Hannaford/The Independent )

She said the brand hired local vendors such as caterers, photographers, yoga instructors, and a tour guide, for the two-day trip. “We had a local woman who lives on the island driving us around, telling us about life there,” Pham said.

“There were events with local people, a luncheon with islanders, and it was nice to talk about what they did there, what they liked about the island, their experience in the summer, and what it’s like in the winter. They also chartered a boat for us and we spoke to a local photographer who grew up on Nantucket.”

Pham says she doesn’t doubt that influencers are taking photos and clogging up the small island streets. “I was totally guilty of that, too. On my trip I had to create content — there's one street that has all these hydrangeas, and people live there, and there were throngs of people taking photos. I woke up at sunrise and was taking shots in the morning on a tripod and I felt so obnoxious. I didn't get in anyone's way, but I could imagine the kind of annoyance that would cause in people's day to day for sure.”

But she said it’s all in the approach. “If you approach it respectfully and encourage people to have a real connection with the place rather than just coming in and using it as a photo set, I think there's definitely ways to make content around a destination in a respectful way.”

Pham said they could highlight local businesses in the area; suggest to their followers they visit a particular coffee shop or restaurant, or offer local recommendations. “At the end of the day the algorithm is only going to push content that is valuable to people - content that is getting those saves, that is getting those shares, because they're offering value to the person consuming it.”

More broadly she believes the term “influencer” reflects people's negative feelings about their relationship with social media and the anxiety that it causes. “I think that people conflate social media with influencers,” she says. “But influencers and content creators are mini media properties; they offer free content, whether that be education, entertainment, recipes, tutorials, tips, reviews, and they need to subsidize that with ads. But I think the ad part angers people.”

Pham said what is almost certainly the real issue in a place like Nantucket is over-tourism. “But the vitriol in the comment sections online make it seem like it's more anger towards social media and the ‘fakeness’ of it and the anxiety that it brings. But they are two different things.

“The same thing is going in [in the small town where I live] — there’s a debate around a moratorium on new development. It's about change. There's always going to be resistance to change, and I think influencers represent change because they're just bringing in new faces and promoting places and bringing in outsiders. These places are usually primarily white and wealthy and so I think that aspect can't be ignored - that the newcomers are maybe more diverse.”

She also points out that young women standing in line to visit Dairy Boy are the same people who in the past would have read an article about a new shop opening up in Vogue magazine. “Maybe they're mistaken for influencers because they have a camera phone — but doesn't everyone have an iPhone these days and take photos? It doesn't mean that you're an influencer.

“I think that's where the kind of the misogynistic angle comes into this,” Pham said. “The word ‘influencer’ is just so gendered and it usually refers to women who are working in the beauty, lifestyle, fashion, motherhood space, and so they see these young women and they conflate them with influencers and social media.”

Perhaps, then, the ‘No Influencers’ sign was not the beginning of a conflict at all, but just its latest, most photogenic iteration. Nantucket has been choking on its own success long before the first tripod appeared on a hydrangea-lined street.

As he drops me off again in the middle of town in time for my ferry back to the mainland, Creedon is sure that, while the over-tourism problem won’t be resolved anytime soon, this brouhaha over influencers — and the influenced — on Nantucket will be a flash in the pan.

“The tide comes in and the tide goes out, and it never stops,” he says. “This will be a thing for a year or two, and then we'll move on to something else.”
