World.title: ‘That wasn’t my son’: Mother of Berlin Pride attacker confronts his turn to terror
World.content:
In the wake of the devastating events of July 25, Abdul Ballout's mother tries to reconcile the son she knew with what authorities have established about his radicalization.

The woman whose son brought terror to Berlin is sitting on a worn red leather couch in a three-room apartment in Berlin’s Tiergarten district. It is Thursday afternoon, and she is pointing to the several missed calls on her phone screen.

They are all from the evening of July 25. They are all from the same person: Abdul Ballout, her son.

“He was terribly afraid for me,” she says quietly, her voice trembling. “I didn’t know why.”

She scrolls through the call log — the last traces of her child from the day of the attack, the day the unknown 21-year-old became the most wanted man in Germany.





She wants the public to get to know him — the son, the brother, the young man that she knew. “I find the way people talk about him incredibly painful, to be honest,” she says. “He was a good person.”

These are the subjective recollections of a mother who cannot and will not accept what her son did — and whose account is difficult to reconcile with what authorities established about him both before and after the attack.

She asks that her name not be published, nor any photograph or recording of her voice.

“I have two other children I have to think about,” she says.

* * *

On the evening of July 25, Ballout drove a rented van into a crowd on the fringes of Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade.

After coming to a stop, he got out of the car and, according to authorities, began attacking people with a machete before fleeing on foot. One person was killed, and at least 29 were injured.

Around 20 hours later, special forces tracked Ballout to a garden in suburban Spandau, where he allegedly attempted to attack officers with a knife when they tried to arrest him. Police opened fire, and Ballout was shot dead. Nine days later, he was buried at Gatow Cemetery in Berlin.

A digital display on a bus stop in Berlin shows the photo of Abdul Ballout on July 26, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

The person killed in Ballout’s attack was a 65-year-old woman from Poland who had traveled to Berlin with her daughter specifically for Christopher Street Day.

Not far away, a gay refugee from Iraq was celebrating at an electronic music event when panic spread through the streets. He had fled a country where being openly gay could put his life at risk. Germany was supposed to be different.

Granted anonymity to speak openly, he said: “For many people, freedom is something they never have to think about. For me, it means being able to love someone, to leave the house in the morning without wondering whether I could be attacked or killed for who I am.”

After the attack, he said, that feeling of safety cracked. “That old fear was suddenly back.”

Sitting across from me just weeks later, Ballout’s mother is dressed in all black, her headscarf framing a face that looks exhausted. There are deep shadows beneath her eyes. She speaks so quietly that at times I have to lean in to hear. The only other sound in the room is the monotonous hum of a fan.





On the coffee table lay empty coffee cups, an open packet of TUC crackers and a box of iron tablets. Propped between them is a framed photograph of Ballout, a faint grin on his face.

She doesn’t want to begin our conversation with the attack; she wants to start with her son. She reaches for her phone and starts showing me videos. In one, he is a little boy in swim trunks, running along a beach and laughing. In another, he is an adult, dancing exuberantly through the living room with his family. He jumps onto the couch and pulls his sisters along, making everyone laugh.

His mother talks of evenings spent together watching television or playing Monopoly, how he would sometimes cheat if he were about to lose. As she speaks, her smiles give way to tears, and her tears give way to smiles.

The contrast with the image of the terrorist could hardly be greater.

* * *

Four days before our interview, I visited the neighborhood where Ballout grew up. Children were crisscrossing a courtyard, neighbors leaning out of windows or standing outside doorways. I asked them about him.

All their answers were strikingly similar: “He always said hello;” “he was polite;” “he was helpful.”

No one disputed what Ballout did. No one tried to excuse it. And yet, no one could explain how the young man they knew was capable of such an act.

German police stand near a white van used in the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

Sitting in his mother’s living room a few days later, her phone rings, and for a brief moment, Arabic singing fills the room. “That’s his voice,” she says. Her ringtone is a recording of her son reciting an Islamic prayer.

But is it just an innocuous recording?

Court records show Ballout repeatedly posted videos containing Islamic State propaganda dating back to 2024, before starting to circulate recordings of his own. In some of the audio files obtained by WELT, which is — like POLITICO — part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters network, he recited the Quran; in others, he appeared to preach. He had hundreds of followers on TikTok and Telegram, with comments praising his voice.

But Ballout’s online messages were radical, speaking of “unbelievers,” God’s “agonizing punishment,” and his rejection of democracy and the German legal system.





Online, he went by the name Abu Muawiyah — a reference to the first caliph of the Umayyad dynasty who emerged victorious over the Prophet Muhammad’s son-in-law Ali and his followers, from which Shiite Islam later emerged. It is also a signal of his shifting faith, as Ballout converted from Shiite to Sunni Islam in 2021.

Was this also a break with his family? His mother gives no indication it was.

She speaks calmly about religion, and without hesitation. She says she was born in Beirut and grew up in Germany. She can neither read nor write Arabic and has therefore never read the Quran in its original language.

German policemen scan the ground of Tiergarten park, near the scene of the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

“I’m not particularly strict about religion,” she says. But her son was different.

For the last several years, he had increasingly been trying to push her toward stricter observance, urging her to pray regularly, to take her religious obligations more seriously and to engage more deeply with Islam.

“He told me every single day how important it was to pray and that it was my duty.”

* * *

Speaking about the days leading up to the attack, one word keeps coming up in our conversation: fear.

Her son had changed, she says. He seemed more nervous, more tense, more restless. He had started changing his phone number constantly — at least five times in 10 days.

“Why are you changing your number again?” she had asked him. But his answer was always roughly the same. Some people kept calling him; he felt followed, harassed and no longer safe.





To this day, it makes no sense to his mother. But to investigators, this is the behavior of someone who had realized he was on their radar — and was planning something big.

In late May 2026, Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office classified Ballout as a high-risk individual capable of committing a serious act of politically motivated violence. And the reasons for this are documented across dozens of pages of case files.

In 2021, Ballout took part in street dawah events organized by a Salafist group in Berlin, where Islamists seek new followers and often distribute copies of the Quran. This is where Berlin’s State Criminal Police Office first took an interest in him.

From 2023 onward, he increasingly frequented mosques influenced by Salafist ideology — which espouses an ultraconservative, fundamentalist view of Sunni Islam — while investigators noted he began openly expressing his rejection of Germany’s free democratic order.

Flowers and candles lie at a makeshift memorial in Tiergarten park on July 27, 2026, two days after the attack. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

In the summer of 2024, he repeatedly posted propaganda from the Islamic State organization, and in May 2025, attempted to join the terrorist group in Africa but was refused entry into Mauritania. Shortly after, he tried to travel to Syria via Lebanon to receive weapons training, communicating with IS members through Telegram.

Lebanese authorities arrested Ballout in July 2025, and a military court sentenced him to three months in prison for incitement to religious conflict. In court, he spoke of two cousins on his father’s side who had died fighting in Syria.

Returning to Germany in November 2025, Ballout was then arrested at Berlin airport and taken into custody on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. According to the case files, he presented himself as a preacher in prison. His religious fervor intensified, and his appearance changed. Ballout’s father later told Der Spiegel that he had argued with his son over his long hair and beard, which he regarded as a sign of religious extremism.





Finally, in May of this year, Ballout was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison but was initially released under the supervision of a probation officer while the court deferred its verdict on whether to suspend the sentence. This judicial decision is now at the center of a heated debate in Germany over how the country handles high-risk Islamist offenders.

From then on, police kept him under surveillance.

Did his mother know any of this? She shakes her head.

* * *

There is only one incident Ballout’s mother is willing to discuss: July 2 this year, his birthday. That day, she says, showed just how closely her son was being monitored.

Ballout had been playing outside with his sister, spraying her with a water gun, she says. Shortly afterward, officers from the State Criminal Police Office appeared. They had assessed the situation as a possible threat.

But investigators describe the scene differently.

It was already dark, and Ballout had stepped outside for just a few seconds, holding what appeared to be a handgun but was difficult to identify, they said. He tucked it into his waistband and went back inside. When officers eventually searched the apartment, they found only a toy gun.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks at the Marienkirche church in Berlin on July 26, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

Investigators believe the 21-year-old was testing whether he was under surveillance — and how much time he had before police would intervene.

And while his mother insists she noticed nothing that would suggest Ballout was preparing an attack, she does not rule out the possibility that others knew of her son’s plans. However, she gives no names.

He spent most of his time with family, she says. He had few friends, at least no one she knew particularly well.

* * *

The day of the attack began, in her memory, just like any other. Both mother and son slept in late, then ran errands. Ballout was unemployed and had no particular obligations, she says. In the late afternoon, he left the apartment before a family gathering that evening.

Then, suddenly, the calls started piling up.

At 5:10 p.m., Ballout called his mother. An hour later, he called again. Then again. Each time, she says, the conversation revolved around the same question: “Are you okay?” He had never done that before.





Then, after one of the calls, she received a short message: “Take care of yourself.”

The words still haunt her today.

At 7:05 p.m., Ballout called again. He asked that his mother inform her partner of over two years that he had a new phone number again. Ballout’s parents have been divorced for three years, but Ballout continued to see and speak with his father regularly, she says. And as the family prepared for the evening, the phone kept ringing.

They were supposed to have dinner at his sister’s place. Schnitzel, his favorite meal, was on the menu. Ballout loved these family gatherings, his mother says. “They always made him happy.” That is precisely why so much of what happened next is incomprehensible to her.

Police investigation marks on the ground near the scene of the attack. | Filip Singer/EPA

“He wanted to live,” she says, her voice rough.

He had spoken of the future, about having a family of his own, about all the things that still lay ahead of him. Nothing had suggested this might be a farewell.

Shortly before 10 p.m., her partner received one more call. They were the last words Ballout deliberately addressed to his family: “Get my mother to safety.”

Minutes later, the van drove into the crowd.

* * *

By the time Ballout’s mother was driven home by her partner that night, the first reports of the attack had started to circulate. At that point, she still didn’t know exactly what had taken place. But when she entered the apartment, she says, something immediately caught her attention.

A key was still in the door.

And right beside it, on the hallway shoe cabinet, were documents that seemed to be deliberately placed where they could not be overlooked. It was the rental agreement for a small van. It listed Ballout as the renter.





“That was when I knew immediately that it couldn’t mean anything good,” she says.

That same night, she took the documents to the police. And as she was questioned, a picture slowly started to emerge — one she initially refused to accept.

At the same time, she kept trying to reach her son, sending message after message. But there was no reply. She only learned the truth the next day, when her daughters called and told her about the reports on the news.

Her son was dead.

Since then, she has spent hour after hour in her Berlin apartment searching for explanations, her thoughts circling endlessly around her son’s last words, his fear and whether there may have been something in those calls that she failed to recognize. She cannot let go of the distorted image she has of her son, of the good boy who wanted to start a family.





Asked what she would say to the victims of the terrorist attack, she thinks for a long time. She is sorry, she eventually says.

“I would also tell them that wasn’t my son.”

Additional reporting by Lennart Pfahler.

Julia Zabert is a trainee journalist with the Global Reporters Network at the Axel Springer Academy. The Academy trains the next generation of leading journalists through hands-on, innovative work with a clear focus on the future of journalism. More information at axelspringeracademy.com.

World.title: The one French politician who’s not on vacation this summer
World.content:
Gabriel Attal, center, shakes hands with a police officer during a campaign visit to Vannes, France on July 25, 2026. | Sebastien Salom-Gomis/AFP via Getty Images

Presidential candidate Gabriel Attal is forgoing the traditional August holiday in a desperate attempt to catch up with his rivals.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is trying to jump-start his presidential prospects by taking advantage of his rivals enjoying France’s cherished August break.

Attal, a former prime minister who now leads President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist political party Renaissance, is betting that by keeping a busy schedule during the holiday and meeting with people across the country — including those at vineyards, markets and ports as well as vacationers in picturesque seaside towns — he can show voters what sets him apart from the field.

“It’s a rather bourgeois assumption to think that all French people take time off or go on vacation,” said a representative for Attal’s team who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about campaign dynamics. “There’s no way he’s going to suspend his campaign over the summer.”



But political reality is also forcing Attal to campaign in August for the vote in April of next year. If he wants a real shot at catching up in the polls, there’s little time to waste.

Surveys have consistently shown the 37-year-old trailing Edouard Philippe, his main ideological rival for centrist and center-right votes. Given the contest goes to a two-candidate runoff if nobody wins a majority in the first round, the two men have tentatively agreed that only one of them should be on the ballot so they don’t split their shared voter base — which could cost both of them a spot in the second round.

Philippe, far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau are all among the presidential hopefuls taking long summer breaks, only interrupting their time off for the occasional op-ed or statement on major events like the wildfires that ravaged southwest France.

Edouard Philippe speaks at a rally in northern Paris on July 5, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images

Their reasoning for slowing down during the peak holiday season is straightforward: Voters want to rest and recharge, so candidates shouldn’t harass them with politics and should instead enjoy one last bit of respite before the race enters its decisive stretch.

“We shouldn’t bother the French people while they’re on vacation,” said a Retailleau adviser.

Attal is betting otherwise that a summer spent campaigning can help close the gap in the polls.

“A campaign is about winning over the French one by one … [Attal] wants to show that he’s more determined than the others,” added his adviser.

The right track

It’s unclear for now to what extent Attal’s summer work will reap dividends with voters, as most pollsters who would investigate that question have themselves set out-of-office messages.

But the absence of other candidates on the campaign trail has given Attal an opportunity to dominate headlines, and he’s used it to make a play for right-wing voters.



At the start of the month, Attal, a member of parliament who represents a Paris suburb, gave an interview to the right-wing weekly Le Journal du Dimanche in which he called for lower immigration, a sweeping streamlining of France’s administrative procedures and more effective enforcement of criminal sentences.

He then traveled to western France, where, in front of cameras, he confronted a group of French gens du voyage — a legal classification for traditionally itinerant communities, including Roma and Manouche, and long a target of the French right — who had occupied land without authorization.

The encounter can be seen below in a report from CNEWS, in French.

French municipalities are required to provide designated stopping sites for traveling communities, but those obligations are not always met — or the sites provided are insufficient — sometimes resulting in unauthorized occupations of public or private land.

For both Attal and Philippe, making inroads on the right will be crucial. Macron’s 2022 reelection was buoyed by older, more affluent voters who had traditionally backed conservatives.

But Philippe begins that contest with a built-in advantage.



He is a former member of the conservative party Les Républicains and has always identified as a man of the right. Attal, who started his political career in the youth wing of the center-left Socialists, has resisted the label.

One conservative minister in the current French government, who has not endorsed a candidate for 2027, readily described Philippe as belonging to his political camp. Attal, the minister said, has a “very flexible” ideological spine.

Sarah Paillou and Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

World.title: Farage paints himself as local Clacton hero in battle to beat Binface
World.content:
One Meta ad suggests he is the only candidate to have visited forgotten areas of the constituency. A further clip shows a local resident giving Farage a positive review of his work — and is presented as proof that opposition complaints he has neglected the patch since his 2024 general election victory in the seat are “cobblers.”

With over 7 million followers across the leading social media platforms — making him by far the most-followed U.K. party leader — Farage has also been churning out election content across TikTok, Instagram and X.

Even with that reach, the Reform UK leader appears to be the only candidate running in Clacton who has used paid Meta features to bolster his online campaign.

Almost £1,000 has been spent on videos of Farage urging local supporters to request the party deliver and install an “I’m with Nigel” garden sign. Meanwhile, around £500 went to ads asking voters to return their postal votes and “send a message to the establishment.”

The largest single sum — between £4,000-£4,500 — was spent on an almost five-minute campaign video in which Farage waxes lyrical about the connection he’s made with local constituents, while claiming his party’s surging success has resulted in the powers-that-be using “foul means” to hamper him.

“Rather than being judged by the political class and the mainstream media, I am going to let you, the voters in the Clacton constituency, make a decision,” he said. “I want you to be my judge, not the political elite.”

World.title: Explosion at Dutch port of Rotterdam leaves one dead and several injured, police say
World.content:
An explosion at the Dutch port of Rotterdam on Thursday killed at least one person and injured several others, city police said.

 

Police said the blast at Europe’s biggest port happened late on Thursday morning and that a crime scene has been set up to try to establish what caused it.

The explosion happened at a refinery and fuel terminal run by Gunvor Energy in an industrial section of the vast port premises.

Dutch broadcaster NOS said that a maintenance team had been working on a section of pipes there.

Rotterdam emergency services reported a major power failure at the port and said that a transformer had caught fire under unexplained circumstances.

A structure in a refinery and fuel terminal run by Gunvor Energy carries the traces of an explosion at the port of Rotterdam, 13 August, 2026 Mouneb Taim/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Several companies halted their operations and evacuated workers.

Power was gradually being restored to companies in an industrial area of the port a few hours later.

A number of oil and gas companies are based there and fire crews were standing by. It was not immediately clear whether the blackout and the explosion were linked.

This is a developing story and our journalists are working on further updates.

World.title: Byway launches free online course to help you plan out a rail trip across Europe
World.content:
Whether you’re an experienced traveller or a total novice, planning out a rail trip can be overwhelming.

 

The EU’s newly announced ‘one journey, one ticket’ proposal should make things a lot easier, but for now, you still have to deal with multiple operators across countries, which can quickly get confusing.

It’s a real barrier to such a sustainable way to get around – and that’s why travel company Byway has just launched a free course teaching people how to do it for themselves.

While it might seem counterintuitive for a company that specialises in booking personalised trips by land and sea for travellers, CEO Cat Jones says the company’s mission is to make no-fly travel mainstream.

“Byway exists to offer the best overland travel experience possible, backed by expert support, fair pricing and free disruption re-planning,” Jones said.

“But whether people book a package through us or book each component part themselves, we don’t want anyone missing out because no-fly travel feels too complex.

“If sharing our expertise means more people skip the airport in this year of heatwaves, then it’s the best ‘bad decision’ we’ve ever made.”

What’s included in the course

The 10-lesson email course, which includes step-by-step videos as well as write-ups, covers everything you need to know about booking a trip by rail.

It includes things like which Interrail or Eurail pass is best for you, how to find rail-friendly accommodation, and how to create a journey guide to manage any unwieldy itineraries.

Plus, it also covers what to do should your journey be disrupted, and how to get your trip back on track.

You can sign up on the Byway website.

World.title: Iran's military rejects Trump's claims of US control over Strait of Hormuz as 'lies'
World.content:
Iran's military rejected as "lies" on Thursday remarks by US President Donald Trump claiming control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strategic waterway was fully under Iranian control.

 

"The false claims of the United States that ships are passing through the Strait of Hormuz normally...are nothing more than lies and fabrications," said Ebrahim Zolfaghari, the spokesperson for Iran's central military command.

"The Strait of Hormuz is, as in the past, under the complete management and control of the Islamic Republic of Iran and no commercial ship or tanker without the permission and supervision of the powerful Iranian armed forces has had and will have the possibility of safe passage through this strait," Zolfaghari said in a video carried by state television.

Iran has kept control of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit, since the outbreak of the war on 28 February, requiring vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the waterway.

In a Truth Social post on Wednesday, Trump claimed that the US "has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!"

A screenshot of a post on US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account, 13 August, 2026 @realDonaldTrump

"Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' and there is nothing Iran can do about it," he added.

On Thursday, the head of Iran's paramilitary Basij forces under the Revolutionary Guards also said that the strait was under Iranian control.

"Today, you see that the Strait of Hormuz is under the management and control of the Islamic republic, and our country continues on its path in complete security," said Hossein Taeb according to state television.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Thursday said the US is making miscalculations in regard to the waterway.

"The US has long miscalculated due to intelligence failures. Case in point: The war on Iran. Now, an even bigger miscalculation on the Strait of Hormuz," he said in a post on X.

Iranian parliamentarian and member of the national security commission Behnam Saeedi said the strait is closed to US and Israeli ships.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrives to meet his Iraqi counterpart in Baghdad, 28 June, 2026 AP Photo

"Ships belonging to the Zionist regime will not have the right to pass through the Strait of Hormuz under any circumstances, whether in war or peacetime," he told state TV, adding that "US military ships will also be barred from passing through the Strait."

Iran and Oman have been in talks to establish a new route through the strait, but negotiations have not yet been finalised.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said earlier this month that Tehran and Muscat were preparing a joint statement on the agreement which includes technical, legal, security and environmental points.

Separately, Iranian media quoted official sources saying that the reopening of the Strait would depend on the US ending its naval blockade of the country's ports.

World.title: Trump’s vaccine overhaul could fuel mistrust and leave Europe vulnerable to disease resurgence
World.content:
US President Donald Trump signed the executive order on Monday, recommending reducing the number of diseases covered by universal routine childhood vaccination recommendations from 18 to 11.

 

Decisions as such could lead to immunisation gaps, leaving populations vulnerable to outbreaks and fuel mistrust in vaccines, Marco Cavaleri, head of the European Medicines Agency’s Public Health Threats Department, told Euronews.

Skipping routine childhood vaccinations could be “catastrophic," he said, adding that it risks “the return of diseases that we were able to contain and eliminate from our countries."

Moreover, it could hamper vaccine trust in society. Such decisions, as the one in the US, “unfortunately, could be very detrimental in terms of vaccine confidence,” Cavaleri warned.

Unpacking Trump’s order

Trump’s order moves recommendations for COVID-19, influenza, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, RSV and hepatitis A and B away from universal routine vaccination. Some immunisations will remain recommended for children considered at higher risk, while others will be subject to “shared clinical decision-making” between parents and healthcare providers.

The order also recommends splitting the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots and administering them at separate visits. Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are currently not available in the US.

The move comes as US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has questioned vaccine safety and promoted claims linking vaccines to autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal association between vaccination and autism.

“The current evidence is unequivocal: vaccines - including the MMR vaccine - are safe and do not cause autism,” World Health Organization (WHO) chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X on Wednesday.

Combination vaccines can also make immunisation easier for children, parents and healthcare workers. Therefore, vaccine development has been moving towards more combination vaccines, rather than fewer.

“So in actual fact, this [US] decision is going against what the future is going to bring to us in terms of getting better protection for children, adults and the elderly,” said Cavaleri, adding that "there is no scientific basis to split these vaccines."

While parents would still be able to choose to vaccinate their children through shared clinical decision-making, health experts warn that requiring separate shots and additional healthcare visits could lead some families to delay or skip vaccinations.

The changes could also reinforce vaccine hesitancy, potentially leaving populations more vulnerable to outbreaks of preventable diseases that have been eliminated or brought under control in many countries.

“Recent changes to US immunisation policy are not aligned with decades of evidence,” said Tedros. “That evidence is reviewed continuously as new data emerge from across the globe,” he added.

The risks for Europe and the globe

Europe has already seen the consequences of falling vaccination coverage. Six countries — Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom and Uzbekistan — were found to have re-established measles transmission in 2024, according to the WHO.

Measles offers a stark example of what can happen when vaccination coverage falls.

“We are already now seeing the return of measles whenever the vaccination coverage gets lower,” Cavaleri said. “And we will see more coming, unfortunately, in the United States and other parts of the world.”

He warned that the situation can get “much worse” if vaccination numbers fall. “Just think about poliomyelitis. Do we want this to come back? I hope not,” Cavaleri said, urging people to vaccinate.

Health experts also warn that the US decision could further undermine public confidence in vaccines also in Europe.

The European Commission’s State of Vaccine Confidence report found that overall vaccine confidence has declined among the general public since 2020, with particularly notable decreases in confidence in many Central and Eastern European countries. US decision could fuel this trend even further.

And the consequences do not stop at borders.

“Europe is the region that we have a duty to look at. But these infectious diseases are causing global problems, global outbreaks, global epidemics,” Cavaleri said.

World.title: Romania shuts off second reactor at Cernavodă NPP amid low water levels on Danube
World.content:
Romania halted operations of its only nuclear power plant on Thursday, a rare shutdown due to a drought scorching Europe that has caused the Danube river, whose waters cool the plant, to fall to record lows.

 

Much of Europe is facing another heatwave this summer amid droughts that have driven rivers to historic lows.

The Cernavodă plant, which usually generates a fifth of Romania's electricity, has been shut down just once before, in 2003, due to drought.

The national nuclear energy company Nuclearelectrica had already shut down one of the plant's two reactors last month and announced on Thursday that it needed to shut the second as well "due to the significant and ongoing drop in the water level of the River Danube."

"We do not foresee a restart within the next ten days," the plant's director, Romeo Urjan, told the AFP news agency.

Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant is seen in Cernavodă, 29 July, 2026 AP Photo

Efforts to divert Danube flow

Romania had been trying to avert a complete shutdown of the plant's two 700MW reactors.

It had budgeted more than €2 million to try to divert the Danube's flow in order to maintain cooling of the reactors, including blowing up a rock and sinking four barges filled with rocks into the river.

Alternative power sources, including from wind power as well as electricity imports, are expected to ensure adequate supplies, the energy ministry said on Wednesday.

But it also reiterated an appeal for "responsible consumption."

The Romanian Navy detonates underwater explosives during a controlled demolition of submerged rocks to improve water flow on the Danube River, 3 August, 2026 AP Photo

It has warned that as a last resort, large industrial consumers would have to face restrictions on consumption in the evening hours to save electricity.

In early August, the government said the carmakers Dacia and Ford would pause production in the country until 19 August to help with the power deficit.

Record-low flows

Nearly two-thirds of the Danube has seen flow rates that are the lowest on record for a month of July in 34 years, according to an analysis published on Monday by the European climate change observatory, Copernicus.

The current drought has been exacerbated by human-induced climate change, according to a report by the World Weather Attribution group of scientists, who warn that the problem is set to worsen.

Neighbouring Hungary has so far been able to avoid a complete shutdown of its only nuclear plant, Paks, whose four reactors are also cooled by the Danube.

People walk on a sandbank on the Danube as usually submerged areas are exposed amid exceptionally low water levels in Rasova, 7 August, 2026 AP Photo

But with the Danube expected to drop even more, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Wednesday that the government had ordered the construction of a submerged wall, or weir, to try to control flows nears the plant.

Two 80-metre barges are also being stationed at Paks that could be sunk to raise the water level.

Paks, whose output usually covers around a third of Hungary's electricity needs, has been partially shut down since late last month.

The low levels of the Danube, Europe's second-longest river, have also severely impacted shipping along its 2,850-kilometre route stretching from western Germany to its mouth on the Black Sea.

World.title: Why do women need 12 times their salary to buy a home, when men need only eight?
World.content:
Home ownership has become much more challenging globally in the last few years. Rising interest rates, persistent inflation and the ongoing cost of living crisis seen in many parts of Europe have made this dream considerably harder to attain for several young people.

 

Soaring property prices and stagnant living wages have added another layer of complexity to this problem too.

According to the European Youth Portal, more than 10% of young Europeans aged 20 to 29 spend more than 40% of their disposable income only on housing costs. This is far above the standard 30% affordability benchmark.

However, women, especially younger, single women, could be at an even greater disadvantage when contemplating buying a home in Europe and the UK, leading to the rise of the gender housing gap.

Why is it more difficult for women to become homeowners than men?

One of the biggest reasons women, especially single women, are more likely to struggle to buy homes than men is due to the persistent gender pay gap still being seen in the UK and several European countries.

In 2024, the gender pay gap in the EU stood at 11.1%, while a Trades Union Congress report released in February this year estimated the UK’s gender pay gap to be 12.8% currently.

Women are also likely to face lower lifetime earnings and higher rates of part-time work, mainly due to more child-rearing, household and caregiving responsibilities, which can severely impact their career progression.

Combine that with the fact that women are less likely to ask for a pay rise according to the European Central Bank, and this creates a vicious cycle that can be very hard to break out of.

As such, they are likely to find it more difficult to save for a house deposit, stamp duty and other repair, renovation and maintenance costs, apart from a mortgage, that usually come with home ownership.

More women are also likely to reduce deposit savings due to financial pressures, while also delaying life milestones such as weddings and starting a family to prioritise saving for a house than men.

The Women’s Budget Group has found that women need over 12 times their annual salaries to be able to buy a house in England, while men need just over eight times. This gap can increase even more when it comes to house prices in key hubs like London.

According to a recent survey by specialist bank Aldermore, 33% of women consider saving for a deposit the biggest obstacle to home ownership, compared to 20% of men.

Similarly, rental costs are likely to hit women harder than men, the survey found, with 76% of women sharing that these costs are a struggle, compared to 67% of men.

As older and middle-aged women are significantly more likely to live alone than men, they also lose dual-income household benefits, making any significant savings and mortgage approvals even more challenging.

This is especially as European women are more likely to experience steeper drops in household incomes after divorces, compared to men.

Splitting a joint marital home can also leave the woman with insufficient capital to re-enter the property market as a sole buyer, redirecting her instead to an ever more competitive rental market.

One of the biggest economic barriers to female home ownership is also that women are likely to get lower maximum loan amounts from mortgage lenders, compared to men, due to these lower per hour and annual salaries.

In many cases, despite having a stable or relatively high income, mortgage holders may view women with part-time or freelance jobs as higher credit risks, which further decreases the chances of loan approval.

Several times, women also face a confidence and knowledge gap in the property market, due to lower financial literacy levels. According to the European Central Bank, only 15% have high financial literacy, compared to 27% of men.

They can also be much more dismissed by brokers, mortgage approvers and estate agents during the buying process, which can make the whole process feel much higher-friction.

Another less considered issue is that several new properties also frequently lack affordable, secure, multi-room housing for single-parent family units, which are overwhelmingly headed by women. This can often lead to them putting off a home purchase for longer, while sticking with renting.

World.title: Russian drone attack on passenger train in Ukraine's Odesa region kills two people
World.content:
A Russian drone struck a passenger train in Ukraine's Odesa region on Thursday, killing two people.

 

The victims of the attack were two crew members, the train machinist and his assistant, the CEO of Ukrainian Railways Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said in a post on Facebook.

None of the passengers were harmed.

"Today in the Odesa region, the Russians once again destroyed an ordinary passenger train locomotive with a jet-powered drone. There were 340 people on the train," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"Whoever was operating that drone certainly could not have been unaware that the target was entirely civilian," he added.

It is not the first time Russia has targeted a passenger train, which Kyiv says is part of an effort to disrupt logistics while increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure.

Russia also targeted port infrastructure in the Izmail district of the Odesa region, local media reported. In total, Russia launched 133 drones at Ukraine overnight into Thursday, targeting 15 locations across the country.

Civilian deaths in Ukraine highest in July since May 2022, UN finds

A recent report by the United Nations revealed civilian deaths in Ukraine hit a record-high in July, the highest since May 2022, the first months of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, a 30 percent increase compared with the previous month and a 70 percent increase compared with July 2025," the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said in a statement on Thursday.

"The number of those killed is the highest recorded since May 2022," it added.

The UN said it verified 16,874 civilian deaths since the start of Russia's invasion, although notes that the toll is likely higher since it cannot confirm casualties in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

Residents leave their damaged home after a Russian air guided bomb strike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko

Kyiv, in particular, has frequently come under fire. At least 54 civilians were killed in the Ukrainian capital during the month of July, the UN said, calling it "one of the hardest hit cities".

Both sides have significantly escalated their long-range attacks this year, causing a spike in civilian deaths, according to the UN.

Ukraine, on its end, has also also ramped up its campaign against Russia's critical and military infrastructure in recent months.

Near-daily barrages targeting Russian oil facilities with long-range drones in recent months have caused fuel shortages, reduced Russia’s refining capacity, and unsettled the Russian public.

On Thursday, a fire broke out at the Gazprom Neftohim Salavat oil refinery, one of the country's largest, in Russia's Bashkortostan Ukrainian media reported.

A fire was also reported at a Wildberries hub nearby. Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, is a critical piece of Moscow's wartime economy.

Ukraine military aid surged in June, boosted by new EU fund

Russia's use of ballistic missiles has proven difficult for Ukraine to intercept, prompting Zelenskyy to call on allies to provide more air defence systems after warning that the country is facing a critical shortage.

Despite long-term shortages, military aid to Ukraine reached its highest level in June since the United States halted funding in February 2025, driven largely by new EU funding, according to data released by the Kiel Institute.

It found that in June, Kyiv was allocated €7.2 billion, the third-biggest monthly military funding boost from donors since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The EU's €90 billion loan was introduced to support Ukraine's budgetary and defence needs in 2026 and 2027.

On top of the loan support, Germany allocated €700 million, Denmark €600 million, and the Netherlands €500 million euros to support Ukraine's military.

World.title: France accues Iran of 'bloodshed' over use of death penalty
World.content:
Following the publication of an international statement condemning the use of the death penalty in Iran, a war of words escalated between senior French and Iranian diplomatic officials. Paris played a central role in the international condemnation, accusing Iran of “bloodshed”, while Tehran in turn described France’s position as “blatant hypocrisy”.

 

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot sharply criticised Iran’s actions in a post on X, writing: “Seven months after the widespread atrocities against the Iranian people who rose up to demand justice and dignity, this regime continues its bloodshed by carrying out an increasing number of executions.”

The French Foreign Ministry also confirmed Paris’s prominent role in the campaign condemning executions in Iran, saying that after the statement was initially signed by 26 countries and the EU’s foreign policy chief, additional countries joined, bringing the total number of signatories to 32.

In response, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi strongly rejected the criticism and accused the French government of applying double standards.

Araghchi wrote on X: "Countries like France should stop lecturing the world about “human rights” and international law. The hypocrisy is blatant and embarrassing."

Iran’s foreign minister added: "Your backing of Israel’s genocide in Gaza—and aggression against Iran—has destroyed whatever moral high ground you imagined you had."

Warnings from international bodies

The diplomatic tensions followed the publication of a joint statement on Wednesday.

More than 30 countries, including France, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany and Italy, along with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, condemned Iran’s use of the death penalty against protesters “in the strongest possible terms”.

The statement said the Islamic Republic was executing protesters in an attempt to “silence dissent”. The signatories said: “The use of the death penalty to intimidate communities and punish people for exercising their human rights is unjustifiable under any circumstances, and the people of Iran must be free to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly without fear.”

The involved countries called on Tehran to immediately end the executions and release those detained.

Economic protests to outbreak of war

The confrontation comes as warnings from the United Nations and human rights groups over a new wave of executions in Iran have intensified.

The latest wave of arrests and judicial sentences dates back to late December last year, when a protest movement initially centred on economic hardship, runaway inflation, the high cost of living and rising prices developed into widespread anti-government demonstrations.

While Iranian officials have reported that more than 3,000 people were killed and attributed the violence to “terrorist actions” organised by the United States and Israel, rights groups outside Iran have reported much higher casualty figures and said security forces opened fire on protesters.

Meanwhile, the joint US-Israeli attack on Iran on 28 February, which marked the beginning of a new Middle East war, further intensified the security crackdown. According to observers, the number of arrests and executions linked to the military conflict and protests has multiplied since then.

The United Nations and human rights groups have expressed concern over the escalation of judicial measures, citing the lack of fair trials and the extraction of forced confessions.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said earlier in August that Tehran was using executions to “spread fear and terror”. He reported that since March 19, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges, while more than 100 others remained at risk of execution.

According to Amnesty International, Iran executed more than 2,150 people last year, placing it a distant second to China among the world’s leading users of the death penalty.

Follow Euronews Persian on X (source in Farsi)

World.title: Ukraine's monthly civilian casualties highest since 2022
World.content:
Published 08/13/2026 Published August 13, 2026 Ukrainian drones strike major Russian oil refinery

Ukrainian drones struck one of Russia's largest oil-refining complexes deep inside the country, according to Ukraine's military, marking the fourth such attack in three days.

Ukraine's General Staff said the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery and petrochemical complex in Russia's republic of Bashkortostan was hit overnight, sparking a fire.

The facility is about 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from the Ukrainian border, southeast of Moscow.

Ukraine's military described it as one of Russia's largest oil-refining and petrochemical complexes.

The plant can process up to 74 million barrels of oil a year and produces gasoline, diesel and other petroleum products.

Kyiv has intensified attacks on Russia's energy sector in recent months, arguing that oil revenues help finance Moscow's war effort.

World.title: How Germany's drone defense fails
World.content:
Drone defense is a priority for the German government. The latest dramatic incident involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport shows there are still substantial shortcomings.

How could a drone laden with explosives fly unhindered into Leipzig/Halle airport, where it remained apparently unnoticed for several hours? After last week's incident, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."

Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because the drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.

The fact that the drone was loaded with explosives and able to reach the airport demonstrates a new level of threat. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.

Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, warned security expert Nico Lange.

"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.

Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.

The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.

Coordinated response difficult for state, federal police

Germany has so far done little to address the issue of drone defense. Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.

In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.

Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.

Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Unclear responsibilities

Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.

Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.

Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.

Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?

As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.

A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.

In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."

From printing to presses to drones To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Airports, train stations still lack protection

There is also lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.

"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."

The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.

The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Eritrea: Key geopolitical player in the Horn of Africa
World.content:
Amid growing tensions and security risks in the Horn of Africa, Eritrea, with its strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, is emerging as an important player in the region.

Across the Horn of Africa, geopolitical interests of various countries continue to cause tensions and conflict as part of the growing competition for political influence over the region.

In its own right, the small country of Eritrea appears to be gaining in importance within this context: The autocratic state run by long-standing ruler Isaias Afwerki controls strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, especially with its ports of Assab and Massawa.

In July, a series of diplomatic consultations in Cairo involving regional powers like Egypt, Somalia, Eritrea, and a high-ranking US envoy highlighted Eritrea's growing role in helping to coordinate approaches to resolving serious security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, and to facilitate trade.

Eritrea's unique location along this maritime route is notably becoming more and more strategic in light of international trade conflicts. The small nation's coastline near the Bab-al-Mandab Strait stretches for more than 1,000 kilometers (621.4 miles), bordering Sudan to the northwest and Djibouti to the southeast.

But Eritrea's main strategic importance relies on who is on the other side of the strait, which at its narrowest point measures less than 30 kilometers.

A small country at a strategically important location

"Yemen lies on the other side of the Red Sea, which makes Eritrea's location particularly interesting, as Yemen is in a state of crisis and maritime security in the region is at risk," Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration (CRI) in London, told DW.

"The only safe route in this area runs through Eritrea, where there are currently no security concerns."

Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki has been ruling the country since its independence in 1993 as a strict one-party authoritarian regime Image: Khalil Senosi/AP Photo/picture alliance

The Houthi terrorist militia, propped up by Iran, have been attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea from the Yemeni coastline.

For the past ten years, Yemen has also been witnessing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in its midst: Ongoing violence, economic collapse, droughts and floods have exacerbated the suffering in the country, according to a report published by the UN Refugee Agency last month.

Sayed meanwhile emphasizes that in Eritrea, the strong dictatorship entrenched for decades does not tolerate any type of dissent. In many international freedom indexes, the African nation often only comes second to North Korea.

Since the country was officially founded 32 years ago, there have been no elections in the one-party state under long-time ruler Afwerki.

A unique sense of stability — for now

But this is also exactly why there are no violent conflicts in the country. Compared to other players in the broader region like Ethiopia, Sudan, and Yemen, Eritrea appears to be an island of peace where it is easy to do business.

"For this reason, all countries — including regional powers such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, which controls the Suez Canal — want to maintain stable relations with Eritrea," Sayed highlights.

At the same time, this could eventually prove to be the country's Achilles' heel: "The country is ruled by a single man, and there are no constitutional institutions. That makes the state very vulnerable should this strongman be removed from power," says Sayed.

There is no strong figure in the 80-year-old autocrat's inner circle seen as a clear successor. This has raised some concern that the security situation could collapse once the president might no longer be in power, according to Sayed.

This sailor from Yemen's internationally recognized government is in charge of controlling activity on the Red Sea Image: Khaled Ziad/AFP

Alternative to the Strait of Hormuz

Still, Eritrea continues to exert its influence as the Red Sea has now emerged as one of the the most important sea route in the world, especially for the Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, according to Sayed.

The war with Iran has further reinforced the nation's position, as this crisis has once again shown the central geopolitical importance of maritime chokepoints such as Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.

One viable alternative, should the Strait of Hormuz remain repeatedly blocked, would be for these Gulf nations and their partners to find routes via Saudi ports located further up on the Red Sea.

While the Saudis have pipelines running from some of the interior regions of the country from where oil is extracted and produced to the port of Yanbu-Al-Bahr on the Red Sea, this alternative route could easily be compromised when it comes to security, potentially driving up oil prices even higher than what they currently are.

"For this reason, Eritrea today is of great strategic importance. This has been the case for centuries and will continue to be the case," Sayed emphasizes.

Why Ethiopia seeks control over Assab port To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ethiopia demands direct Red Sea access

Meanwhile, Eritrea's neighbors, particularly landlocked Ethiopia, are fighting hard to maintain access to the Red Sea as a trade route, Sayed adds, in particular for oil exports from the Horn of Africa to the rest of the world, especially to Europe and the Americas.

For decades, Djibouti has dominated regional trade logistics as Ethiopia's most important seaport partner, while Eritrea has been sidelined economically.

But Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has for years been demanding sovereign access to the sea — more than three decades after the country's split with Eritrea: when Eritrea gained its independence in 1993, Ethiopia lost its direct access, and has since been relying on its neighbors for all its sea trade.

However, maintaining a sense of neutrality and balance is proving to be a walk on a tightrope: Earlier in 2026, the fragile relations with between Ethiopia and Eritrea's Asmara region had already threatened to escalate amid a dispute over Ethiopia's access to the maritime trade route.

Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The key context for Eritrea's recent strategic maneuvers in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea is the escalating tensions with Ethiopia," says Michael Woldemariam, a researcher at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland and the Atlantic Council.

"Asmara is seeking to forge partnerships that can serve as a counterweight to Addis Ababa. Its recent diplomatic outreach to Egypt, Somalia, the United Arab Emirates' armed forces, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopian opposition groups, and even the US should be viewed against this backdrop," he tells DW.

Meanwhile, a new trade corridor on the Red Sea is also taking shape: In May 2026, Eritrea and Egypt signed an agreement to establish direct freight connections between Egyptian and Eritrean ports on the Red Sea to expand independent trade and supply chains in the region.

A grave record of human rights violations

Still, there are no long-term guarantees with Eritrea, since the country's short history is almost entirely marked by violence, resulting in many people seeking a better life elsewhere.

"The first people fled Eritrea for Sudan in 1967 to escape [former Ethiopian ruler] Haile Selassie's imperial army. In the 1980s, people fled in large numbers from the Ethiopian military dictatorship. Since 2001, people have once again been fleeing in large numbers from human rights violations, military service, war, and a lack of prospects," says Magnus Treiber, a migration researcher specializing in the Horn of Africa at the Institute of Ethnology at the University of Munich.

"The causes of flight have hardly changed. However, since the European Union now offers virtually no opportunities to seek asylum, Eritreans are now fleeing all over the world."

Displacement is rife around the Horn of Africa, where various conflicts repeatedly force entire populations to seek safety elsewhere Image: GIULIA PARAVICINI/REUTERS

At least 700,000 people have left the country since its founding, which is about a fifth of its total population. The country's population growth, meanwhile, is under 2% — a low number compared to many countries in the region.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: What would a North Korean surge mean for Ukraine war?
World.content:
Ukraine is claiming that North Korea is preparing to send tens of thousands more troops to Russia, where they'll gain valuable battlefield experience. President Zelenskyy has urged South Korea to work closer with Kyiv.

North Korea is preparing a massive troop surge to help its ally Moscow in its war on Ukraine, with up to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed in Russia, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

In late July, the Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops, before adding this weekend that Pyongyang decided to have between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans deployed on Russian territory. He did not specify if this number included the North Korean troops already taking part in the conflict.

In the comments published this weekend, Zelenskyy also warned North Korea was gaining valuable experience in modern warfare and urged South Korea to boost cooperation with Ukraine on air defense and drones. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia.

North Korea has suffered thousands of causalities in Ukraine war

Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later. Analyst believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region.

Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded.

This image, published by Ukrainian officials, shows North Korean soldiers being fitted for Russian uniforms Image: Ukraine Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front.

Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality'

South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer.

Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country.

"I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war against Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment.

"Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military."

Will North Koreans watch Russians' back?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, also seemed to signal caution.

"Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW.

"North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han.

"Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to front-line combat in Ukraine."

Russian officials praise North Koreans

"North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said.

North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean causalities, some 2,000 may have been killed.

"Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment," Han said.

"North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery."

North Korean women also moving to Russia

Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops."

"North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979.

"If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added.

Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel."

Ukraine war used as training ground for North Korean military

According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military."

"However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn.

"A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden."

Kim hails troops returning from Russia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Germany: Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive
World.content:
Rail traffic was suspended in a region of Bavaria and authorities evacuated buildings around a train station after a suspicious object was found on the tracks. Police later confirmed it did not contain explosives.

Buildings near a train station in the southern state of Bavaria were evacuated as a precaution on Thursday after police said that an object found on the tracks could contain explosives.

Investigators later determined that the object was not an explosive, although criminal police were continuing work at the scene.

A technician had discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen.

Specialists X-rayed the object, which was also lifted using a robot to allow further investigations.

A federal police bomb disposal team is examining the object Image: Felix Kirberg/dpa/picture alliance

Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged.

Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes.

08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Steel giant Thyssenkrupp plows on with Duisburg production, for now, despite Rhine river issues

In less dry summers, like last year, barges piled high with coal would service Thyssenkrupp's facilities in Duisburg Image: Jochen Tack/picture alliance

German steel giant Thyssenkrupp says the low Rhine River levels have not yet impacted production at its major facility in Duisburg.

Chief Financial Officer Axel Hamann said that supplies to customers were not presently at risk, as he presented nine-monthly performance figures to the press.

For the moment, he said, the facility was still receiving some deliveries of raw materials — particularly coal for the furnaces — via partially-laden barges on the Rhine.

"If the situation really deteriorates and the ship journeys are stopped altogether, then we could not rule out an effect on results," he said, meaning sales volumes and output.

"We of course do have a few options to adapt the production and the deliveries to our facilities somewhat, so we can continue to work longer with the supplies that we have," Hamann said. He said there were shipping alternatives and that the company was trying to secure more supplies via rail in particular.

"We're still a long way away from letting some of our furnaces run cold," Hamann said.

Boats with smaller cargo loads can still access the Duisburg steelworks, but the channel is far shallower than usual with the banks exposed entirely in places. This was the situation in mid-July, when levels were slightly higher than at present. Image: Jochen Tack/picture alliance

The company was also looking into potential transport by road networks, he said — but typically coal is seen as a very bulky, heavy and cost-inefficient product to transport using trucks in large quantities. Earlier in the week, a company spokeswoman had suggested that truck transportation was not a realistic option.
