World.title: EU report: Human rights and democracy in Georgia deteriorated significantly in 2025
World.content:
EU report on Georgia — 2026

According to the European Union’s annual report for 2025, the human rights and democracy situation in Georgia deteriorated significantly. Laws adopted by the government and its repressive measures further restricted fundamental freedoms.

Overall, the report portrays Georgia as a country where the weakening of democratic institutions, restrictions on fundamental rights and shrinking space for civil society are closely interconnected.

The report says the country’s EU integration process has effectively stalled, while much of Brussels’ financial and political support now goes to civil society and independent media rather than the government.

What does the report say?

Freedom of expression, assembly and association

The report says Georgia has restricted freedom of expression, assembly and association, as well as the rights to equality and protection from discrimination, respect for private and family life, liberty and personal security.

The document highlights widespread reports in 2025 of law enforcement officers mistreating protesters. According to the EU, some cases amounted to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment. The report says no one has been held accountable for such incidents, contributing to a climate of impunity.

The EU says arbitrary arrests, excessive use of pre-trial detention and disproportionately harsh sentences handed down to protesters and journalists raise serious concerns about the right to a fair trial.

The report also examines cases of physical violence, sexual harassment, rape and death threats against women taking part in demonstrations.

Media restrictions

According to the EU, new legislation adopted by the Georgian government has made it even harder for independent media and civil society organisations to operate. The report highlights amendments to the laws on broadcasting and “transparency of foreign influence”, as well as a legislative package concerning family values and the protection of minors.

The report also notes numerous reports of intimidation, threats, verbal abuse, physical violence and arbitrary detention targeting journalists and other media workers.

The European Union says the government’s repressive measures against civil society, the media and the opposition have significantly undermined democratic processes. They have effectively reduced public participation in political life and weakened the effectiveness of checks and balances.

The EU also highlighted the freezing of bank accounts belonging to several civil society organisations as part of the use of judicial mechanisms to suppress dissent.

Political pluralism has also deteriorated. The report notes an attempt by the ruling party to have several opposition parties banned through the Constitutional Court.

According to the EU, Georgia’s declining democracy indicators are also reflected in international rankings. The country ranked 114th in Reporters Without Borders’ 2025 World Press Freedom Index, 52nd in the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index and 56th in the Corruption Perceptions Index. It also scored 34 points on the CIVICUS Monitor, indicating a shrinking space for civil society.

According to the EU, new legislation adopted by the Georgian government has made it even harder for independent media and civil society organisations to operate. The report highlights amendments to the laws on broadcasting and “transparency of foreign influence”, as well as a legislative package concerning family values and the protection of minors.

The report also notes numerous reports of intimidation, threats, verbal abuse, physical violence and arbitrary detention targeting journalists and other media workers.

The country ranked 114th in Reporters Without Borders’ 2025 World Press Freedom Index, 52nd in the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index and 56th in the Corruption Perceptions Index. It also scored 34 points on the CIVICUS Monitor, indicating a shrinking space for civil society.века, который не велся с июня 2023 года, также не был возобновлен», — говорится в докладе.

Financial support for civil society

The statement notes that, amid democratic backsliding, the European Union extended its suspension of direct financial assistance to the Georgian authorities for 2025. At the same time, EU funding went towards supporting civil society and independent media.

Under the NDICI programme, €24 million was allocated to directly support civil society and independent media, with a further €10 million allocated for 2025–2027 under the Eastern Partnership Civil Society Facility.

Existing EU programmes cover areas including improving access to justice, protecting the rights of people with disabilities and children, and safeguarding the rights of ethnic and religious minorities and the LGBT community. They also support gender equality, efforts to combat disinformation and strengthening the institution of the Public Defender.

ECHR and international obligations

The EU report also takes a critical view of Georgia’s cooperation with the European Court of Human Rights and its implementation of the court’s judgments.

According to the document, the level of cooperation and compliance with court rulings was deemed insufficient. A total of 45 cases remain under enhanced supervision by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe.

The EU also identified problems in Georgia’s cooperation with international organisations. The Georgian authorities did not issue an invitation to the OSCE observation mission in time to allow full monitoring of the municipal elections scheduled for October 2025. They also failed to take adequate steps to implement the organisation’s previous recommendations.

The report also notes that, despite retaining its seat on the UN Human Rights Council, Georgia has not joined several important international and EU initiatives.

World.title: Irakli Kobakhidze: “‘Deep state’ is trying to artificially fuel Russophobia in Georgia”
World.content:
“Radical anti-Russian sentiment in the country is being artificially fuelled and is part of a new campaign against Georgia,” Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He said attempts to intensify Russophobia in Georgia were part of a plan carried out by agents of the “deep state”.

Kobakhidze recalled that the Georgian government had repeatedly said that, after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, the so-called “global war party” had tried to draw Georgia into the conflict and open a “second front” in the country.

The prime minister said this “window of opportunity” created an “existential threat” to Georgia and its population. He said calls for Georgia to join international sanctions against Russia soon followed. According to the government, complying with those demands would have had serious consequences for the country’s economy.

“Because the Georgian government refused to comply with these demands, pursued a sovereign policy and acted in the interests of the state, our country became a target for the European bureaucracy and Western leaders working in tandem with informal oligarchic forces,” Kobakhidze said.

He also addressed the sanctions imposed by Western countries on the Georgian government. According to Kobakhidze, pressure mechanisms, including sanctions, were already being used when the previous US administration under Joe Biden was in power.

Kobakhidze said the sanctions had targeted senior Georgian government officials, ruling party honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, judges, senior police officers and others.

He said the West had also used Georgia’s EU membership prospects as a tool to pressure the government.

“They failed to break the ruling party, which enjoys the support of the Georgian people, so now they are trying to use their agents to drag Georgia into a new provocation,” he added.

Kobakhidze said a “new stage of the attack” on Georgia, its people and its sovereignty had begun:

“This is a qualitatively new stage of the attack on Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s sovereignty, unfolding simultaneously on several fronts.”

Background

Several days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy letter addressing the issue of “Russophobia”.

In the letter, Kobakhidze discussed the links between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic political situation and the opposition’s position. He said the “global war party” benefited from the ongoing conflict in Ukraine because it wanted to “fuel Russophobia at the highest level among its agents around the world, including in Georgia”.

Kobakhidze accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current tough stance towards Moscow as “Russophobia”.

The letter reignited political disputes over the events of the 2008 war. This time, however, the debate focused not only on the circumstances that led to the war and Russia’s responsibility. The prime minister shifted the focus from Russia’s actions to the position of his Georgian opponents.

Georgian PM on “Russophobia”

World.title: Ilham Aliyev’s AzTV interview during Nakhchivan visit: industrial park, energy projects and Zangezur Corridor
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

On 11 August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. It was Aliyev’s 17th visit to Nakhchivan since he became president.

During the visit, officials held foundation-laying ceremonies and opened several facilities. Aliyev also visited historical sites and presented battle flags to military units.

The visit ended with an interview with Azerbaijan Television (AzTV), in which Aliyev outlined his plans for Nakhchivan’s development.

The interview focused on the autonomous republic’s economic and social development, energy security and transport infrastructure. Aliyev also discussed Nakhchivan’s place in Azerbaijan’s broader strategy, particularly its future development in conjunction with Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, territories that came under Baku’s control after the Second Karabakh War.

Key events during the visit

During the visit to Nakhchivan, President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva inspected work at the Shams-1 and Garbi Ufug solar power plants, which have a combined capacity of 50 MW.

One of the key events was the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan Industrial Park. It will be Azerbaijan’s second-largest industrial park by area, after the Sumgayit Industrial Park. A 300 MW thermal power plant is also planned for the site.

Nakhchivan’s total generating capacity currently stands at around 200 MW. Once the new plant comes online, this will increase by roughly half.

The visit programme also included:

the opening of the Nakhchivan Regional DOST Centre;

the presentation of new electric buses and an inspection of railway infrastructure reconstruction works;

the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan hotel complex, which is expected to be completed by around 2028;

the laying of the foundation stone for a social housing complex;

an inspection of restoration work at the Momine Khatun Mausoleum and the unveiling of a monument to architect Ajami Nakhchivani;

the presentation of Nakhchivan’s General Development Plan through 2044, which envisages expanding the city and increasing its population;

the presentation of battle flags to new commando units of the Separate Combined Arms Army.

Key points from the AzTV interview

Aliyev described his visit to Nakhchivan as a “sign of the autonomous republic’s comprehensive development”. He said every visit should produce concrete results. He highlighted strengthening defence capabilities, energy security, job creation, preserving historical and cultural heritage, and developing transport links as key priorities.

Defence and governance

Aliyev said Nakhchivan’s geographical position – particularly its lack of a direct land connection with mainland Azerbaijan – requires special attention to the region’s defence. He highlighted the creation of the Separate Combined Arms Army and new commando units as key steps.

According to the president, “Azerbaijan’s Armed Forces carry weight in the region”. He also said Nakhchivan had introduced a system of special presidential representatives, similar to the model used in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur. Aliyev said the benefits of this system of governance were already becoming apparent.

Energy

Nakhchivan has been fully supplied with gas for around 15 years, Aliyev said, thanks to a gas swap agreement with Iran.

The president also placed particular emphasis on the region’s solar energy potential. He said Nakhchivan was Azerbaijan’s most favourable region for solar power generation. More than 600 hectares of land have already been allocated for the development of this sector. The potential is estimated at at least 500 MW and could reach 1 GW in the future.

Aliyev also highlighted the growing role of the private sector. Projects to build solar power plants with a combined capacity of 50 MW are already under way.

The president described electricity exports as a strategic priority. Iran and Turkey are currently the main destinations, but Azerbaijan ultimately hopes to export electricity from Nakhchivan to the European market as well.

Zangezur Corridor – TRIPP

Aliyev said that “the creation of the Zangezur Corridor was our initiative”, recalling that connecting mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan, an integral part of the country, had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

He said he had insisted that a provision on the corridor be included in the trilateral statement signed by Azerbaijan, Russia and Armenia on 10 November 2020. Aliyev claims the Armenian side did not want to agree to this, but had no other alternative because continuing the war was not in its interests.

Noting that there had been no practical progress on the issue for five years, Aliyev said a solution emerged after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025, when the TRIPP project (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) was launched.

Speaking about the current state of the work, the president said the Horadiz-Aghband highway was almost complete, with only minor technical issues remaining. He said construction of the railway was also progressing rapidly.

Aliyev added that a project for power transmission lines linking mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenia had already been prepared, and locations for the pylons had been identified.

Aliyev predicted that these projects would eventually turn Nakhchivan into one of the region’s key transport and energy hubs.

A unified development concept

The president stressed that Nakhchivan, Eastern Zangezur and Karabakh should develop under a unified concept. He said the geographical proximity of the three regions requires a common approach to their development.

Aliyev noted that master plans for cities in the territories that came under Azerbaijan’s control after the Second Karabakh War had already been approved. He also said he had ordered the preparation of a similar document for Nakhchivan. The “Nakhchivan City Development Master Plan through 2044” was presented to the president during the current visit.

Speaking about the region’s tourism potential, Aliyev said Nakhchivan had significant opportunities thanks to its rich historical heritage, scenic landscapes and clean air. At the same time, he acknowledged that the hotel infrastructure remained underdeveloped and that the existing hotels were generally of a low standard, hindering the growth of tourism.

He said that to address the problem, construction had begun on a new five-star hotel complex in the city centre. The project is expected to be completed around 2028.

Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

World.title: Child seats, rear-seat seat belts and alcohol interlocks: changes to Georgia’s traffic rules
World.content:
New road safety rules in Georgia

Georgia plans to tighten road safety rules under the National Road Safety Strategy for 2026–2030, approved by the government on 5 August 2026. The strategy includes changes in several areas.

At this stage, the measures remain proposals, and some will require further legislative amendments before they can take effect.

What is changing:

Child seats will become mandatory for pre-school children. This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt.

This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt. Rear-seat seat belts could become mandatory. The government strategy provides for mandatory seat-belt use by passengers sitting in the back. However, authorities must first establish the necessary legal framework and an enforcement mechanism.

The government strategy provides for mandatory seat-belt use by passengers sitting in the back. However, authorities must first establish the necessary legal framework and an enforcement mechanism. Drunk drivers could be prevented from driving. The strategy provides for the introduction of so-called “alcohol interlocks”. These devices check a driver’s blood alcohol level and prevent the car from starting if it exceeds the permitted limit.

The strategy provides for the introduction of so-called “alcohol interlocks”. These devices check a driver’s blood alcohol level and prevent the car from starting if it exceeds the permitted limit. Georgia plans to establish a standard for alcohol-based ignition interlock systems. Under the strategy, authorities intend to take alcohol interlock technology into account when setting requirements for vehicles entering the Georgian market. The strategy does not, however, call for the immediate installation of such devices in all vehicles in the country.

Under the strategy, authorities intend to take alcohol interlock technology into account when setting requirements for vehicles entering the Georgian market. The strategy does not, however, call for the immediate installation of such devices in all vehicles in the country. Measures to detect drivers under the influence of drugs will be strengthened. The government plans to introduce specialised technical equipment in stages to help detect drug use among drivers. Interior Ministry officers will also undergo additional training to improve the detection of drug-impaired drivers.

The government plans to introduce specialised technical equipment in stages to help detect drug use among drivers. Interior Ministry officers will also undergo additional training to improve the detection of drug-impaired drivers. Electric scooter rules could be revised. The strategy calls for a detailed review of existing legislation governing the safe use of electric scooters. The review should lead to recommendations on possible changes. No specific new rules have been announced at this stage, although additional regulation remains under consideration.

The strategy calls for a detailed review of existing legislation governing the safe use of electric scooters. The review should lead to recommendations on possible changes. No specific new rules have been announced at this stage, although additional regulation remains under consideration. More attention will be paid to pedestrian safety, including children’s safety. The strategy calls for road safety to be incorporated into pre-school education programmes and for educational materials to be developed for parents and children. Authorities also plan to run awareness campaigns for pedestrians on the importance of following traffic rules.

The strategy calls for road safety to be incorporated into pre-school education programmes and for educational materials to be developed for parents and children. Authorities also plan to run awareness campaigns for pedestrians on the importance of following traffic rules. Infrastructure will be adapted for vulnerable groups. Future infrastructure projects are expected to give greater consideration to the safety of people with disabilities.

The government strategy says seat-belt use is one of the key ways to reduce deaths and serious injuries in road accidents. It pays particular attention to rear-seat seat belts because unrestrained passengers in the back can endanger not only themselves but also people sitting in the front of the vehicle.

The strategy is not limited to introducing new requirements. The government also plans to raise awareness of road safety, run public campaigns and educational programmes, and improve technical tools for detecting violations.

It is important to note that the government strategy sets out some of these measures only in broad terms. Where necessary, authorities will have to introduce additional legislative and regulatory amendments to implement specific commitments.

World.title: Ukrainian defector to Russia killed in bomb attack, Kyiv targets oil refinery
World.content:
A Russian military officer has been killed in a bomb attack in Sevastopol — the largest city in Russian-annexed Crimea — and a woman arrested on suspicion of assassinating him on behalf of Ukrainian special services, the regional governor says.

Several unofficial Russian Telegram channels on Thursday named the victim as Robert Shageyev, a former Ukrainian naval officer who switched allegiance to Russia during Moscow's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine. But Myrotvorets, an unofficial Ukrainian website that provides a database of people described as war criminals or traitors, said Shageyev had been "liquidated".

Five killed, oil refinery closed after Ukrainian attacks on Russia

Separately, regional governor Mikhail Razvozhayev said five people were killed in Sevastopol overnight during an operation to dispose of an explosive device.

He said four emergency service bomb disposal specialists and a security guard were carrying out clearance work following a Ukrainian drone attack on the city when the explosion occurred.

Sevastopol Governor Mikhail Razvozhayev said a Russian officer was killed in a bomb attack and five others were killed in a separate incident. (AP: Gavriil Grigorov)

Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defence units shot down or intercepted 362 Ukrainian drones overnight across a number of Russian and Russian-controlled regions, including Crimea, which Moscow seized and annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Both sides have scaled up their attacks in the fourth year of the war which has raged since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with Ukraine increasingly targeting oil refineries and retailer warehouses in an effort to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war.

An oil refinery in the Russian city of Orsk that was hit by a Ukrainian drone strike two days ago has been forced to shut down completely, and repairs could take up to six months, the regional governor said on Thursday.

"Shrapnel damaged key infrastructure that cannot currently be repaired. The equipment is imported, and due to sanctions, repairs could take up to six months. The plant has completely shut down," Yevgeny Solntsev, governor of the surrounding Orenburg region, posted on social media.

" We are preparing for a worst-case scenario and will have to rely on fuel supplies brought in from outside the region. "

The Ukrainian military said on Tuesday it had attacked the Orsk refinery, located near the border with Kazakhstan about 1,470 km south-east of Moscow, and set it on fire.

Russian strike on Ukrainian passenger train kills two

A Russian drone attack on a train carrying hundreds of passengers in southern Ukraine killed two people on Thursday, Ukrainian officials said.

"Today in the Odesa region, the Russians once again destroyed an ordinary passenger train locomotive with a jet-powered drone. There were 340 people on the train," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

"Whoever was operating that drone certainly could not have been unaware that the target was entirely civilian," he added.

None of the passengers were harmed, the chief executive of the state railway operator said.

Two people died in the Russian drone attack on a train in Odesa, Ukraine, officials said. (AFP: Odesa Regional Military Administration)

A video published by the Ukrainian emergency services showed a bright fire raging in the train cab, the front of which was blown out and mangled.

Moscow's forces have repeatedly targeted trains throughout the war, in what Kyiv calls a campaign to cut off logistics and hit civilians.

The United Nations also said on Thursday that the number of civilians killed in Ukraine in July jumped to its highest level since the first months of the Russian invasion.

"At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, a 30 per cent increase compared with the previous month and a 70 per cent increase compared with July 2025," the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said in a statement.

" The number of those killed is the highest recorded since May 2022. "

Following the attack, Mr Zelenskyy repeated his call for "more air defence support and more pressure on Russia" as concerns mount that Ukraine is running out of interceptor missiles.

He previously told CNN that Ukraine needed five per cent of the United States' Patriot interceptor missiles to get through the winter.

"If they can sell us 10 per cent, we will destroy all the Russians' ballistic missiles," he said.

261 bodies of soldiers returned to Ukraine, 24 to Russia

Russia and Ukraine swapped bodies of killed soldiers on Thursday.

Ukraine's drone attacks on Russia could backfire Ukraine is firing drones deep inside Russian territory almost every day since June, but some analysts argue it could give Vladimir Putin an excuse to escalate his war.

"The bodies of 261 deceased persons have been returned to Ukraine, which, according to the Russian side, belong to Ukrainian servicemen," Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said in a statement.

Kyiv has previously accused Russia of including the remains of civilians and Russian soldiers in the exchanges.

Citing a Russian lawmaker, the RBC media outlet also said Moscow had handed over 261 bodies, while Ukraine had transferred 24.

The exchange of bodies and captured prisoners of war are some of the only areas where the two sides conduct diplomacy and reach agreements, more than four years since Russia invaded.

ABC/wires

World.title: Defence pact for Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia open to expansion
World.content:
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will group senior ministers, hold joint exercises and deepen defence industry cooperation under a military pact signed between the regional powers last week, Türkiye's defence ministry says.

The three Sunni Muslim US allies, alarmed by a regional conflagration that has brought Iranian missile fire onto Gulf oil exporters, signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7.

They said the accord stipulates that an armed attack against any member would be regarded as an attack on all, similar to NATO's Article 5 collective defence clause.

At a weekly briefing in Ankara on Thursday, the defence ministry said the pact's fundamental goal was to ensure defence and military ties were put on a "more institutional and sustainable" footing.

Unpacking a NATO-like defence pact A NATO-like defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan has landed like a stone thrown into an already rippling Middle East pool.

"Under the accord, strategic political and military mechanisms plan to be established involving the defence ministers, foreign ministers, and chiefs of general staff/armed forces commanders, and that coordination among the three countries will be conducted at the highest level," it said.

The ministry added that joint military exercises involving land, naval and air forces — as well as air defence and unmanned systems — were planned, in addition to deeper defence industry cooperation.

"The aim is to provide not only product and system supply, but also joint development and production, technology cooperation, and sustainable maintenance and logistics support," it said, adding that unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence capabilities would be prioritised.

Türkiye, which has NATO's second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion — with Egypt as a potential candidate — and did not seek to replace any existing alliances.

The ministry also said Türkiye was participating in meetings in Jeddah aimed at establishing an international coalition to protect Red Sea shipping.

Reuters

World.title: Foreign minister to link diversity to national security
World.content:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong will use a high-profile speech on Friday to declare that the rise of populism threatens Australia's national security, saying the "melancholic fantasy of monoculture" risks making Australia "lonely in a dangerous world".

Senator Wong will deliver the annual Gyngell Lecture — which is named after the revered policy stalwart Allan Gyngell who died in 2023 — at the Lowy Institute in Sydney.

It comes as Labor continues to struggle in the polls, with Pauline Hanson and One Nation remaining politically ascendant, despite increasingly sharp scrutiny from other political parties and the media.

One Nation has vowed to slash foreign aid and withdraw Australia from multilateral institutions if it wins power, while Senator Hanson has taken aim at corruption among Pacific leaders.

Pauline Hanson has called for Australia to become "monocultural". (ABC News: Adam Kennedy )

Senator Wong will not mention the party by name in her speech, but will make multiple clear references to One Nation's core policies, arguing that isolationism will impoverish and isolate Australia.

"Denigrating our region and neglecting our partners is no way to secure Australia's interests," she will say.

"Neither is encouraging some kind of retreat from the world and the institutions that go with it."

Most Australians say diversity positive

This year's Lowy Institute poll shows Australians are increasingly unhappy with migration levels, with 55 per cent saying the total number of migrants coming to Australia is "too high" — as well as a sharp drop in the number of Australians who support cultural diversity.

But 73 per cent of those polled still said they see diversity as "entirely" or "mostly" positive, which Senator Wong will say shows the nation still retains faith in the multiculturalism, even if social cohesion is "under pressure".

What is 'monoculturalism' and what does it look like in practice? Pauline Hanson has called for Australia to reject multiculturalism and be "monocultural". So what does it involve and are there any nations overseas that show what it might look like in Australia?

Senator Hanson has called for a return to "monoculturalism", although she insists that the term is not racially discriminatory and simply requires migrants of all faiths and backgrounds to embrace Australian values.

Senator Wong will argue this vision is not just at odds with the reality of modern Australia but will also leave the nation adrift in Asia, and "lonely in a dangerous world".

"I've always believed the ability of Australians to connect with people from every part of the world is a national asset … an asset that expands our choices in the world," she will say.

What One Nation’s foreign policy looks like With One Nation running red hot in the polls and posing a serious challenge to the incumbent parties, there's more scrutiny on what its foreign policy would mean for Australia.

"The call for a monoculture is a call for Australia to curtail our choices and cut off our connections … to look inwards, to have no friends to work with, no partners to trade with, no opportunities to grow from."

She will also argue that a poisonous debate over diversity could also stoke social resentments and division in Australia.

"Well before we could ever realise this melancholic fantasy of monoculture, there is a lot of damage that can be done," she will say.

"Because Australians would be turned against each other. Australia would be a more hostile place. Harder to be family, harder to be a friend, colleague, or neighbour."

A warning against division

The foreign minister will also suggest that fuelling division will make Australia more vulnerable to disinformation campaigns from "external" forces — although she will not point the finger at any foreign states.

Researchers have previously accused some authoritarian states — including China and Russia — of running disinformation campaigns aimed at fracturing social trust in Australian democracy and driving narratives more favourable to them.

"At a time where external and internal forces are seeking to divide us, turning Australians against each other makes us more vulnerable," Senator Wong will say.

"Division makes us easier to exploit, it doesn't make us stronger."

World.title: Shots fired as men with machetes argue at Melbourne shopping centre
World.content:
Police have converged on a shopping centre in Melbourne's north after shots were fired during an argument between men armed with machetes.

Craigieburn Central was placed into lockdown at around 7:10pm on Thursday.

Police were told two groups of males, both armed with machetes, were seen arguing at the shopping centre and two gunshots were heard.

Martin was at the centre with his six-year-old son.

He said he saw a group of males wearing masks just outside the food outlet where he was sitting.

He said some men approached the group and it looked like they were telling them to calm down when a second group of masked males arrived.

"They ran towards each other and then a shot was heard," he told the ABC radio program Evenings with David Astle.

"As soon as the shot was fired … everybody pulled out massive machetes.

"They looked like swords; I've never seen such large machetes before."

Martin said he immediately called the police while other shoppers fled.

He said there were mainly women and children inside the food outlet.

"Almost every single one of them were on the floor.

"I picked up my son, and I saw a lady with her four daughters. Roughly about five or six minutes later, when everything calmed down, they were too scared to leave."

A Victoria Police spokesperson said the offenders fled as officers arrived.

She said there had been no reports of any injuries or any evidence to suggest anyone was hit by the bullets.

Police are investigating the incident and urged anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

The ABC has attempted to contact shopping centre management.

World.title: Bulgarian coastal city Burgas to host Eurovision 2027
World.content:
Burgas, a Black Sea city in Bulgaria, has been chosen to host next year's Eurovision Song Contest.

The final of the world's biggest live televised music event will take place on May 15, 2027, the organisers announced on Thursday, local time.

Key takeaways from Eurovision 2026 Slept through Eurovision this year? Here's what you missed from Europe's favourite song contest, in Vienna.

It will be the first time that the Balkan nation hosts the contest after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year's contest in the Austrian capital Vienna with the catchy floor-filler Bangaranga.

"The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and Bulgarian National Television (BNT) are excited to reveal that Burgas has been selected to host the 71st Eurovision Song Contest in May 2027," they said in a press release.

The semi-finals will take place on May 11 and May 13.

Burgas edged out capital Sofia to stage next year's contest after a "complex" evaluation "covering all EBU requirements", BNT general director Milena Milotinova told a press conference.

Burgas is the second-largest city on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, with a population of about 190,000.

An important commercial port, it is also one of the main gateways to seaside resorts along the coast, including Sunny Beach, a prime tourist destination for its golden sands.

'An honour'

The contest will be held at Arena Burgas, a multifunctional venue with 5,500 seats that can host up to 15,000 people.

Burgas mayor Dimitar Nikolov said it was "an honour and a privilege" to be chosen.

"Thank you for the unique chance to present Burgas, the region, and the beauty of Bulgaria. We will give it our all to perform at a high level and be remembered as a successful host," he said.

It is hoped the contest will provide a boost for the tourism sector, which accounts for about 8 per cent of GDP in one of the EU's poorest countries.

Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform since its launch in 1955, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame as well as boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.

Delta 'proud' to be at Eurovision as five nations boycott competition This week, the Eurovision Song Contest will burst onto the stage in Vienna, and onto screens around the globe, but behind the colour and campness, this year's competition is shaping up as one of the most politically charged in history.

The 2026 competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down 35 million on the year before after five countries boycotted it over Israel's participation.

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the contest — with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all.

Eurovision Song Contest organisers also announced that they were excluding any country in an armed conflict from hosting the competition and increased the minimum age of competitors from 16 to 18.

While they did not mention any country by name, Israel, which has been at war in Gaza since 2023, came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.

Bulgaria debuted in Eurovision in 2005 but had never won the contest before Dara's 2026 victory.

The EU country on the Black Sea had missed the last three editions of the glitzy extravaganza for financial reasons but took the crown in Vienna after overtaking Israel at the very end.

AFP

World.title: Senator says NT doesn't 'want to stick to' terms of $4b housing deal
World.content:
The federal and Northern Territory governments are in a deadlock over a multi-billion-dollar project to build thousands of new homes in remote Aboriginal communities, with concerns the project could deliver fewer than half the number originally planned.

Jointly funded in 2024, the NT Remote Housing agreement is aimed at reducing overcrowding and improving housing quality in the Territory's Indigenous communities, town camps and homelands.

PM announces $4 billion NT remote housing package Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced the 10-year agreement, which is expected to see up to 270 homes built each year, during a visit to the Northern Territory.

The $4 billion project promised to deliver 2,700 new homes over 10 years, but the NT government has recently asked to renegotiate the agreement.

In federal parliament on Wednesday, Senator Lidia Thorpe tabled documents she said showed $330 million in Commonwealth funding due under the agreement "has not been delivered and the Northern Territory government has provided no progress reports".

"Building is behind schedule, construction targets are being reduced, reporting is missing, funding isn't flowing, and mob are telling you that NT is not working for them," she said.

On Wednesday, Lidia Thorpe tabled documents and shared her concerns over the housing plan for the remote NT. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Federal Indigenous Australians minister and senator for the NT, Malarndirri McCarthy, said when the NT government "meets certain criteria, then [it] will receive the funding".

Senator McCarthy told parliament the NT's Country Liberal Party (CLP) government wanted more money from the agreement and that it "wants to reduce the number of homes down to 1,800 or maybe 1,100".

"They don't want to stick to the agreement," she said.

"They want to remove a certain amount of money from it for administration and for the land, in terms of where the houses will be built, in terms of making sure the land is ready."

'Pressures' on the NT

NT Housing Minister Steve Edgington was contacted for comment but did not respond by deadline.

Late last month, Mr Edgington told ABC Radio Alice Springs that 400 houses had so far been built under the agreement, but that he could not detail how much had been spent to build them.

Steve Edgington has previously said the NT government faces a variety of pressures that impact on its ability to deliver on the agreement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

He argued more money was needed to cover additional costs because "what we're facing at the moment is a whole range of different pressures on the program".

"We've seen significant increases in cost due to the global fuel crisis — around construction, freight, fuel, labour, infrastructure — and all those servicing costs have increased substantially, not just over the last 12 months, but in the last six months," he said at the time.

"Some of the costs are anywhere between $300,000 and around about $600,000, just to bring a block on to have that ready to build a house on.

"So these costs, which include the headworks, the power, water, sewage, all of those things which are essential components to build a home, are escalating out bush at the moment."

Senator Thorpe told the ABC she backed the federal government in rejecting the NT government's proposal to redistribute funds from the agreement for administration and headworks.

She called for Senator McCarthy to dump the NT government from managing the project and to instead directly fund Aboriginal organisations to do the work.

Lidia Thorpe wants the government to directly fund Aboriginal organisations to do the work in remote communities. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"The Northern Territory government need to basically move over and the minister needs to step in and bypass, which she has the power to do, and fund these organisations directly," she said.

" Then houses can be built immediately. "

'Serious concerns' among committee members

The documents tabled by Senator Thorpe also included a joint statement from the Aboriginal members of the agreement's Joint Steering Committee, dated September 2025.

These Australians are homeless with a house Many Aboriginal people in Tennant Creek live in overcrowded makeshift shelters with no running water or electricity as they wait up to a decade for a home. But experts say the social housing being built is not safe for today's climate, let alone the future.

In it, the members said they held "some serious concerns about the approach of the [NT government], in particular the Department of Housing", and called for the Indigenous Australians minister to "intervene where [the CLP] are falling short and hold them accountable".

The members' concerns included a "lack of clear reporting from the department and a reluctance to share data", along with "repeated comments by the department around the lack of capacity to do anything more than business as usual" on improving repairs and maintenance in the remote NT.

The statement said the Aboriginal committee members had "diminishing confidence that the department has a long-term strategic vision or has the capacity and willingness to change the way they currently do business".

The ABC understands the Joint Steering Committee — which is comprised of representatives from both governments, Aboriginal Housing NT and the four NT land councils — is due to meet next week.

World.title: Third Sydney Airport take-off incident investigated by safety body
World.content:
Safety authorities are investigating a third runway incident at Sydney Airport involving a Qantas flight crossing the path of a departing Virgin Australia aircraft.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said on Wednesday that the incident on Sunday involved Virgin Australia Flight VA555 destined for Perth and Qantas Flight QF728 flying to Ayers Rock Airport.

"At around 10am local time, air traffic control (ATC) cleared the Virgin Australia 737 for a full-length take-off on runway 34L," an ATSB statement said.

Radar mapping of Sydney Airport on August 9 shows Virgin Australia Flight VA555 awaiting take-off at 10:05am while on a runway. (Supplied: FlightRadar24)

"As the crew applied thrust for take-off, they observed the Qantas 737 begin to cross the runway ahead of them from taxiway Lima.

"The Qantas crew reported having received a clearance from ATC to cross the runway.

"The Virgin Australia crew reduced thrust and the aircraft came to a stop on the runway."

At the same time, Qantas Australia Flight QF728 could be seen approaching the runway from an adjacent taxiway. (Supplied: FlightRadar24)

The ATSB said air traffic controllers cancelled VA555's take-off clearance at the same time its crew noticed the Qantas aircraft ahead.

"Once the Qantas 737 was clear of the runway, the Virgin Australia 737 was re-cleared by ATC to commence take-off," the ATSB said.

It is understood the Qantas plane began to cross the runway about 1,200 metres ahead of where the Virgin Australia flight had started to take off, before its clearance was cancelled four seconds later.

The ATSB said it would conduct interviews with the crew involved and review recorded flight data as part of its investigation.

Air Services Australia said the two aircraft were never in close proximity and it was working with the Australian Transport Safety Bureau to investigate the incident.

Aviation boss summoned, airport workers stood down after Sydney near-miss Australian Transport Safety Bureau's Chief Commissioner Angus Mitchell says pilots who avoided a near miss at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning "prevented what could have been far more serious".

Spokespeople for Qantas and Virgin Australia told the ABC the airlines would support the ATSB investigation into the incident.

In another incident earlier on Sunday, Jetstar Flight JQ402 was preparing to take off when it was forced to slam on the brakes to avoid colliding with a Qatar Airways 777 that was being towed along the tarmac.

ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said on Monday that the Jetstar incident "could have been far more serious" if the pilots involved had not been quick-thinking.

He said those sorts of runway incidents "shouldn't happen".

"We do have an aviation sector that is the envy of the world. That's not to say that with incidents like this, we don't take them seriously to improve," he said.

"But aircraft movements, whether it be in a busy airport or in the skies, are incredibly well coordinated here in Australia."

Two airport workers were stood down temporarily following the near collision, which left a Jetstar crew member injured yesterday.

Two weeks earlier, on July 27, a QantasLink flight and a Qantas plane were involved in a near-miss on the tarmac.

Recent workforce shortages and rostering issues have contributed to delays at Sydney Airport.

World.title: Roosters force first NRL lead change in five months
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have moved to the top of the NRL ladder for the first time in five years, leapfrogging Penrith with a 12-6 win over the Panthers.

With three rounds remaining, the Roosters are in the box seat to win the minor premiership thanks to a two-try showing from Daly Cherry-Evans and an electrifying performance from his halves partner Sam Walker at Parramatta Stadium on Thursday night.

Walker this week parked contract extension talks with the club until after their finals campaign and his clear mind helped Trent Robinson's men gain just their second win over Penrith in 14 meetings since the start of 2020.

The Tricolours produced a strong defensive performance in the highly-anticipated clash. (Getty Images: Matt King )

Cherry-Evans opened and finished the scoring and still looks every bit an NRL player as rumours swirl that the 37-year-old playmaker will head to the Super League for a career swansong next year.

The Roosters, who have won their last eight consecutive games, face Wests Tigers, the Dolphins and South Sydney to round out their regular season.

Penrith, meanwhile, could drop out of the top two by the end of the weekend after being the competition leaders since Round 4.

In their first hit-out since losing captain Isaah Yeo to a pectoral injury, Ivan Cleary's side lacked direction in attack and have now lost five of their past eight games.

The Panthers went desperately close to opening the scoring with a 14-pass move putting Brian To'o in the clear to touch down, only for the winger to step in to touch at the last minute.

The Roosters remained camped in their own half until a wayward Nathan Cleary pass fell to Mark Nawaqanitawase to relieve the pressure on Robinson's side.

In an instant, the Tricolours were up the other end and Cherry-Evans burst past a flat-footed Isaiah Papali'i to score in the 20th minute.

Walker converted and the Roosters should feel aggrieved for not doubling their lead as halftime approached when Rob Toia had a try chalked off.

Nawaqanitawase was penalised for a disruptor penalty that Canterbury football manager Phil Gould described in commentary for the Nine Network as "a disgraceful call and a disgraceful rule".

Walker kicked a penalty goal on halftime after a push and shove between Dylan Edwards and Connor Watson to make it 8-0 at the break, condemning Penrith to a scoreless first half for the second week running.

The Panthers were lacking spark, but with 15 minutes left Ivan Cleary threw Blaize Talagi on at five-eighth and they immediately reacted to the shake-up.

After pounding the Roosters' line, Lindsay Smith slipped an offload away to fellow forward Moses Leota who powered over with a 67th-minute try.

Cleary kicked the conversion to make it 8-6, but the Panthers were unable to come up with a late knockout blow as Cherry-Evans scampered over with a 77th-minute match winner.

AAP

World.title: Chillin’ in the City of Gold
World.content:
Ken Arnold of Leura can back up Rhoda Silber’s remark about the incongruous snow situation in Johannesburg (C8). “I can recall what was probably the same occurrence, around September 1981. A colleague in Johannesburg decided that, being the dry season, it was the ideal time renovate their roof. The day after removing the roof, it didn’t rain – it snowed.”

Going by the experience of David Fletcher of Pymble, it had happened before: “My first sighting of snow was in Joburg in August 1962 as a 4-year-old. My first snowman didn’t last too long as the snow melted by lunchtime!”

Paul Jameson of Suffolk Park writes: “My first sight of snow was when I was 8 (70 years ago) and living in the foothills of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. That magnificent mountain always had its snow cap but unfortunately, it was not fashionable to climb it. I was back there last year and saw very little snow left, another effect of climate change. I’m now too old to climb Kilimanjaro.”

“While staying in Dirranbandi, Queensland, we were approached with a question from other travellers from Brisbane about the ‘white stuff’ on the side of the road,” recalls Janice Creenaune of Austinmer. “‘Cotton’ we replied. They’d thought it might be snow but were in too big of a ‘rig’ to stop and investigate on the one-lane roads.”

“Silent Movie (C8), Mel Brooks at his best (C8),” remarks Brett Jack of Bonnyrigg Heights. “An all-star movie with only one word of dialogue in the entire film - ‘Non!’, and that word uttered by none other than mime maestro Marcel Marceau. Brilliant!” Serge Nemaz of Illawong agrees and hopes Herman Beyersdorf forked out for the headphones: “Definitely worth the $2, I would think!”

World.title: ‘Weaker at home’: Wong’s veiled warning to One Nation on national security
World.content:
PoliticsFederalForeign relations ‘Weaker at home’: Wong’s veiled warning to One Nation on national security Natassia Chrysanthos August 13, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Foreign Minister Penny Wong will paint Pauline Hanson’s call for a monoculture as a major threat to national security, making the case that Australia’s diversity is a bulwark against global instability while reaffirming that regional diplomacy is Labor’s top priority. Wong will argue that her own Malaysian background demonstrates how migrants have enriched Australia and helped it find common ground with other people in the world, also pointing to Burundi refugee Nestory Irankunda and his opening goal of the Socceroos’ recent World Cup campaign. Foreign Minister Penny Wong listens to an address at the National Press Club last month. Dominic Lorrimer Her speech comes after a charged debate over multiculturalism was spawned in June by Hanson saying Australia should be monocultural. The One Nation leader later backtracked, saying the diverse Socceroos football team was an example of what she was talking about. Labor has since worn multiculturalism as a badge of pride as it seeks to counter Hanson’s surging popularity, and Wong’s speech will take this a step further by making the direct link between diversity and successful foreign policy.



“Our multicultural society, along with our economy and our democratic institutions, are essential elements of our resilience and raise the costs for those who seek to coerce us,” Wong will say in a speech to the Lowy Institute on Friday. Related Article Protests ‘We are not stupid kids’: Perth students rally against Pauline Hanson “And those who seek to divide us for clicks and votes should know that they make us weaker at home and more vulnerable in the world.” Wong will argue this is increasingly important given rising global instability, with China’s military buildup and recent ballistic missile tests in the Pacific, and United States President Donald Trump’s war with Iran. She will say Australia’s multicultural make-up gives it particular currency in the Indo-Pacific region, since more than a million Australians trace their families to South-East Asia, and more still to South and North Asia.



“No other country I have visited can meet this region so naturally on its own terms,” Wong will say. “We are more prosperous because of our diversity. We have more choices because of it. We are more capable in the world, and we are more able to find common ground with so many of the world’s peoples because of it.” The Albanese government has re-oriented Australian foreign policy since coming to power, focusing on regional relationships in South-East Asia and the Pacific while building alliances outside the United States to shore up its strategic influence as a middle power. Australian foreign policy has historically centred on the US alliance, regional engagement and a rules-based order, but Wong last year shifted this formula to put the region first and add another pillar of “resilience” to Australia’s diplomatic priorities. Expanding on this approach on Friday, Wong will say: “The first priority must be the region, because this is where Australia has the most on the line.



“The second priority is relationships. It is not enough to exclusively champion the alliance. Our priority since coming to government has been to diversify our relationships, while strengthening traditional partnerships with the United Kingdom and the United States. Related Article Foreign relations Japanese ambassador moves to quash melon drama, defend Albanese “We have always understood that President Trump envisages a different role for the United States in the world. Even so, the United States remains the world’s largest economic and military power, with daily influence over international events that have consequences for Australia.” Wong will point to Australia’s ability to secure fuel and supplies from Asian neighbours when the Strait of Hormuz was closed due to the US-Iran war earlier this year as evidence this strategy had been successful. She will also reference a range of pacts recently signed with Indonesia, Timor-Leste, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu, Tuvalu and Nauru to argue Australia had made “transformational breakthroughs” in building regional security.



“These agreements help us contribute to a strategic balance of power in our region ... Those relationships must be reinforced, thoughtfully, deliberately and continuously, by every part of government, businesses and the community. Security is everyone’s responsibility,” she will say. But these would be undermined by talking down the region or retreating from global institutions, Wong will say, in a thinly veiled reference to Hanson. “The ability of Australians to connect with people from every part of the world is a national asset,” she will say. “The call for a monoculture is a call for Australia to curtail our choices and cut off our connections … To look inwards, to have no friends to work with, no partners to trade with, no opportunities to grow from. To be lonely in a dangerous world.” Wong will warn that damage to the country will be done “well before we could ever realise this melancholic fantasy of monoculture”.



“Because Australians would be turned against each other. Australia would be a more hostile place,” she will say. “At a time where external and internal forces are seeking to divide us, turning Australians against each other makes us more vulnerable. Division makes us easier to exploit, it doesn’t make us stronger. Turning Australians against each other is the opposite of patriotism. “Our resilience starts with how we choose to live together... It starts with respecting that multicultural Australia is the only Australia that has ever existed.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Codie Taylor to captain All Blacks for first time against Bulls
World.content:
Hooker Codie Taylor has been named All Blacks captain for the first time. He will lead the team in their third tour match in South Africa against the Bulls.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie is also handing Josh Jacomb the reins at first-five while Beauden Barrett drops to fullback.

Taylor returns from injury to captain the All Blacks in his 110th match and first of the tour.

Props Xavier Numia and Tyrel Lomax will also play their first matches of the tour.

Six players from the All Blacks team who beat the Sharks 54-0 on Tuesday are back up for the Bulls match, including lock Josh Lord, loose forward Wallace Sititi, halfbacks Kyle Preston and Cortez Ratima, midfielder Timoci Tavatavanawai and outside back Emoni Narawa.

The final hit-out before the first test against the Springboks, Rennie said this looms as an important game for the All Blacks.

"The Bulls have consistently been South Africa's best franchise side, making the United Rugby Championship finals in four of the last five years. Loftus Versfeld is one of the most formidable rugby grounds in the world, so we are aware of the challenge in front of us and excited at what lies ahead."

Rennie said Taylor was a natural leader of the squad and an easy pick for skipper.

"He is a top man and has done a great job leading this tour group. This is a proud moment for an All Blacks centurion who has made a massive contribution to this team."

The All Blacks are playing at Loftus Versfeld Stadium in Pretoria. They have played there 16 times since 1928, including four games against the forerunner to the Bulls, Northern Transvaal, in 1949, 1960, 1970 and 1976.

The All Blacks won the first three games and lost the 1976 match 29-27.

Kick off is at 5am Sunday 16 August NZT.

World.title: Passengers rescreened, flights delayed after potential security breach at Auckland Airport
World.content:
A potential security breach at Auckland Airport this afternoon resulted in passengers on a flight being rescreened.

The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said an aircraft had to return to the gate at the domestic terminal after a passenger entered the secure departure area through an exit door before boarding

As a precaution, passengers were disembarked and rescreened, and the aircraft was searched before being returned to service.

Some flights were delayed while these procedures were completed.

"This incident was not the result of a failure in Aviation Security screening processes. Initial enquiries indicate the passenger gained access to the secure area by using an exit door," a CAA spokesperson said.

"Working alongside airport and airline staff, Aviation Security officers needed to make sure the area was secure before normal operations could resume.

"The safety and security of passengers remains our priority."

Enquiries were ongoing.

An Auckland Airport spokesperson said passengers from one domestic flight were rescreened by Aviation Security after a potential security breach.

"No other flights were impacted. Safety and security are our priority and we thank travellers for their patience," they said.

World.title: Armed man shot dead at Auckland mall known to police
World.content:
A man has been shot dead at the country's largest shopping mall after fleeing officers in an incident that sparked a major response from emergency services.

Auckland City District Commander Sunny Patel said police received information of an air rifle theft from a gun retailer in Penrose that sparked a chase.

Workers locked themselves and others inside their stores and parts of the shopping complex were put into lockdown.

For those inside Sylvia Park, uncertainty turned to terror and fear as workers reported screaming and police with guns who were moving customers and telling them to lock their doors.

Dozens of police cars converged on the shopping complex in Auckland's Mt Wellington and patrol cars with their lights still flashing remained scattered across the sprawling car park more than two hours later.

Nandan, a manager at the mall's Timberland store, was locked inside his rear storeroom after quickly realising that what he thought was people having fun was anything but.

"Like I was sitting there in my back room, like having my lunch and waiting for my next meeting, and suddenly I've heard a few people screaming," he told RNZ's Checkpoint.

"And I've heard a weird sound, and I just about came out and two of my staff came running inside the back room and saying 'did you hear it? It's people are shooting, like there's a shooting," he said.

Armed police at Sylvia Park shopping centre. Supplied / RNZ

"And as soon as I went close to the main door, the main gate, I've seen a policeman there and other people are running in front of the Timberland and JD [store]".

"And then suddenly police, uh, uh, ask us, and uh, one of my colleagues, to lock the door," Nandan said.

"And since then, we are sitting here, uh, back in the back room, uh, not going on the floor, and waiting for next instruction from police."

Others also reported what sounded like gunshots.

One retail worker said armed police locked down half the mall and turned people away.

Police had put up a white sheet outside the mall in the afternoon. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

He said he was concerned for his staff's safety and that people in stores nearby were feeling anxious. "I'm not going to lie ... some of them are very antsy."

Another worker said he was in a storeroom when he heard yelling over the radio.

Other employees told him they had seen a man running and heard multiple shots - between four and five but could not agree.

"It's really horrible," he said

People outside the mall after police had arrived. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

He said he saw helicopters, fire trucks, police cars and officers with black vests through the store window, and staff locked their doors and stayed inside.

Hato Hone St John said it was alerted shortly before 3pm and sent an ambulance and other vehicles.

Later, police were seen outside the Footlocker store holding up a white sheet.

Police vans began arriving to help carry out investigations.

Police initially released few details, but said there was no risk to the public.

Just before 6pm, police said an armed man fleeing them had been shot.

"Earlier this afternoon, at around 2pm, police received information about a theft of an air rifle at Gun City in Penrose," Supt Sunny Patel, the Auckland City District Commander said.

"The offender has fled in a vehicle and units have been dispatched. The Police Eagle helicopter deployed to the area and has located the white Suzuki Swift travelling near Sylvia Park."

Patel said the vehicle was tracked going into Pakuranga and they then saw it being driven erratically towards Panmure.

"Units successfully deployed spikes as the vehicle continued towards Panmure. The vehicle continued towards the Mount Wellington Highway, still being driven in an erratic manner."

A Suzuki Swift is towed away from outside the shopping centre. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

It was outside Sylvia Park the vehicle got stuck, Patel said.

"At this point, approximately 2.50pm, the offender fled on foot carrying a long-barrelled air rifle. He has run on foot onto the grounds of the shopping centre.

"Units have pursued the offender as he headed towards an entrance into the shopping centre. Whilst still in possession of the air rifle, he has been confronted underneath an overpass where he was been shot by police."

Police said first aid was given straight away but the offender died at the scene.

Emergency services outside Auckland's Sylvia Park mall. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"Police have now stood up a critical incident investigation into the events that have unfolded this afternoon. Our investigation is still in the very early stages of piecing together all the events."

Speaking to media at around 7pm Patel said the man was known to police but not wanted.

Patel confirmed the man was under bail conditions but had not breached those conditions.

He would not go into details about the identity of the deceased man, saying the next of kin had not yet been notified and police were planning to do so on Thursday night.

He encouraged anyone with information or footage to come forward and said the ongoing investigation will look into details including how the rifle was stolen, whether it was loaded and what the potential intentions of the man were.

One witness told Stuff they saw armed police chasing after a person before shooting him down outside Footlocker.

"They follow the guy and then they shoot him. Three shots, he was dead."

The witness said they had initially seen the man that would be shot, run past them.

"He was just running... I couldn't tell what his intentions are, I'm sure they weren't great."

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The witness told Stuff they could tell something was wrong.

"There was a pistol in his hand but I kind of didn't find that out until later.

"Knowing that he was so close to me with a gun even is just kind of scary, but he looked like a normal dude."

As darkness fell, cars that were initially stuck behind expansive cordon tape began being allowed out while inside the large mall, shopping continued.

A large barricade was put up inside blocking shoppers from the area of interest on what would normally be a late night of shopping on a Thursday.

World.title: Cook Islands election: preliminary results starting to come in
World.content:
Preliminary results are starting to come in for the Cook Islands general election.

As of 10pm local time, preliminary results indicated the incumbent prime minister and Cook Islands Party leader Mark Brown had easily won the Takuvaine-Tutakimoa seat.

Brown had 269 votes, while the next best placed was Davina Hina Te Raurea Joan Hosking-Ashford of the Democratic Party with 103.

In other preliminary results for leaders of the main parties, Teariki Heather, the leader of the United Party won the Murienua seat with 320 votes, more than double that of the second placed Cook Islands Party candidate, Nooroa Baker.

In an upset, the Democratic Party leader Tina Browne - the opposition leader in the past term - has lost Rakahanga by just three votes to Levi Hitarahera Teinaki of the Cook Islands Party who had 24 votes.

Preliminary results indicate Tina Browne has lost her seat. supplied

There are 11,000 registered voters in the Cooks, and voting stations opened at 9am on Wednesday morning, Cook Islands time (11am Thursday NZT) and closed at 6pm.

There are 24 constituencies in the Cooks, 10 on the main island of Rarotonga, and the other 14 spread across the Pa Enua, or outer islands. Thirteen seats are needed for a majority to form a government.

A total of 63 candidates were confirmed for the 2026 general election, down from the 71 who contested the 2022 election. This year's lineup includes 49 men and 14 women.

With independents making up 20 per cent of candidates, should no party claim the 13 seats needed for majority, the independents could hold the power over who forms government.

There's been a delay in the Northern Cooks, as bad weather meant electoral officers were unable to get ashore in Nassau.

Officials have announced the island's polling will be postponed to Thursday afternoon local time.

World.title: Vietnam's 'most powerful leader' since Hồ Chí Minh visits New Zealand
World.content:
The prime minister says there is clear direction for the relationship between New Zealand and Vietnam, following a visit by Vietnamese president Tô Lâm.

Vietnam is New Zealand's 13th largest trading partner, with two-way trade valued at $3.41 billion in the year to March 2026, an increase of 72 percent over five years.

Lâm has been president since April, as well as General Secretary of the Communist Party since 2024 - essentially holding the top two positions in Vietnam's political hierarchy.

Last year, the two countries upgraded their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, to coincide with 50 year of diplomatic relations.

Now, with Lâm's visit to Auckland, several areas of co-operation have been boosted.

Describing Vietnam as "a rising star of Asia", Luxon said there were huge opportunities for the countries to work closer together.

Dairy, fruit, and wood are New Zealand's biggest exports to Vietnam, while its biggest imports include electrical equipment, travel, footwear, and machinery.

The upgrade sees New Zealand able to sell more honey, deer velvet, and venison to Vietnam, while New Zealand would have access to more Vietnamese flowers and foliage, such as carnations, daisies, orchids, and lilies.

The two also signed a fresh memorandum of arrangement, to increase cooperation in agriculture, fisheries, and forestry.

"It's really important for us to be in there on the ground floor as it grows and as it becomes wealthier. That creates huge opportunities," Luxon said.

Luxon visited Vietnam last year, and called in on Lâm in Hanoi.

Since then, Lâm has been re-appointed to the presidential role, a position he also held in 2024, whilst also holding onto the general secretary role.

Following their meeting on Thursday, Luxon described Lâm as "probably the most powerful leader in Vietnam, I'd say, since Hồ Chí Minh," and his state visit, the first by a Vietnamese president since 2007, was a marker of the strength of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

A joint statement was released by Christopher Luxon and Tô Lâm. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The joint-statement released by the two leaders said they recognised the elimination of non-tariff barriers to "enhance the impacts of our free trade arrangements to businesses and consumers".

Vietnam, like New Zealand, has been affected by the United States' tariffs, and Luxon said the relationship showed the "massive diversification" countries were showing to look elsewhere for trading partners.

"Trade is highly local. It's actually our exporters in regional New Zealand selling produce into Vietnam they previously couldn't do. As that country gets wealthier, there's a greater demand for our products and services, and of course that money comes back home, and is then spent in the local economy, creating jobs and further income."

World.title: Dome Valley landfill proposal returns to court over river rules
World.content:
A controversial landfill proposal for north Auckland is back in court, with Forest and Bird challenging the development over its impact on rivers.

Waste Management New Zealand proposes building and operating the 80-hectare landfill in Wayby Valley, near Dome Valley and Wellsford.

In 2021, an Auckland Council independent commissioner panel granted conditional approval for the landfill. That would have seen 12km of streams destroyed within the footprint of the landfill.

The decision was appealed to the Environment Court by iwi, conservation, and community groups.

In 2023, the Environment Court issued a decision allowing the landfill to go ahead.

Forest and Bird appealed that decision, focusing on the relevance of river protections. That was heard at the Court of Appeal on Thursday.

Lawyer for Forest and Bird Martin Smith said it was agreed that the effect of the loss of 12.2km of streams could not be mitigated.

Waste Management New Zealand had proposed mitigating it through plantings alongside 50 to 60km of streams in the Hōteo River catchment and beside on-site streams, as well as through compensation.

Smith said the debate was about whether the significant effects could be offset or compensated.

He said the location of the landfill was also relevant, and that a landfill did not need to be located over a river to function: "It's not a hydro dam, it's not a port."

Forest and Bird did not accept statements that there was no better alternative site, Smith said.

Waste Management's lawyer Bal Matheson KC said the company had relied on offsets and compensation to reduce the level of impact to below material harm, and if there was no material harm then the rivers policy did not apply.

"We say it's entirely appropriate to offset and compensate."

Avoiding all effects was unreasonable and an inappropriate interpretation of the rules, he said.

As for the location of the landfill, Matheson said Waste Management took 10 years to select the site, avoiding places identified as high value ecological areas in the Auckland Unitary Plan.

Opponents of the proposed landfill protest in central Auckland in 2020. RNZ / Jogai Bhatt

He said he wasn't sure why the company was being criticised for building a landfill outside of a high value overlay.

Representing Ngāti Manuhiri, Jason Pou told the court the landfill proposal would allow hapū that had been historically dispossessed to rebuild their rohe and revitalise themselves by standing on their own land.

"There's a real impact on Ngāti Manuhiri in this in terms of their future generations," Pou said.

The new landfill was initially proposed to replace the company's Redvale landfill, which was consented to accept waste until December 2028.

Waste Management was seeking fast-track consent to expand Redvale Landfill and continue operations there to 2036. Minister for Infrastructure Chris Bishop granted the application for referral to the fast-track process in April.

Waste Management has also applied for referral to the fast-track process for its Wayby landfill. If referral is granted, the fast-track process would run alongside the court process.

The appeal was heard by Justices Jillian Mallon, Matthew Palmer and David Collins.

Justice Mallon said they were conscious of the need for a reasonably prompt decision.

They reserved their decision.
